docs.text: Today you join the analytics team of Cordillera Mobile, a Chilean mobile carrier with thousands of customers and two urgent questions. By the end of the class you will describe a customer in Python, apply the retention team's first rule to a list of customers, and open the real customer base for the first time. ≈ 85 min 9 ideas Runs in your browser Advance 1
docs.title: Day one at Cordillera Mobile

docs.text: Welcome to the team. Two messages are already waiting for you: the commercial team asks: "What drives a customer's monthly bill?" the retention team asks: "Which customers are about to cancel, and who should we call?" Over five sessions you will answer both, with Cordillera's own data. The tool is Python , written in a notebook : a page that mixes text cells (like this one) with code cells you can run. On this site, each code cell has a Run button and Python runs right in your browser. In Google Colab you press ▶ or Shift + Enter. A code cell is a calculator that remembers. Run the next one. In [1]: Copied! # Anything after a # is a comment: Python ignores it. monthly_bill = 31.9 # one customer's last bill, in USD print ( "This customer pays" , round ( monthly_bill * 12 , 2 ), "USD a year" ) # Anything after a # is a comment: Python ignores it. monthly_bill = 31.9 # one customer's last bill, in USD print("This customer pays", round(monthly_bill * 12, 2), "USD a year") This customer pays 382.8 USD a year Python now remembers monthly_bill , so any later cell can use it. That memory (the kernel ) belongs to the session, not to the page: it only knows what you have run, in the order you ran it . Run cells out of order, run one twice, or delete one, and the memory no longer matches what you read on screen. Try it below. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Business takeaway: your notebook is a report that others will rerun. Before you share it (or hand in an advance), use Runtime → Restart session and run all in Colab ( Run all on this site). If it runs top to bottom without errors, your teammates and your grader will see exactly what you saw.
docs.title: 01 Your first day

docs.text: Let's describe one customer, CM-10482, the way the billing system does: a plan, a bill, how long they have been with us, and whether they pay automatically. Each fact gets a variable : a name on the left of = , a value on the right. A variable is a label , not a box: the value lives in memory and the name points at it. When you write tenure_months = tenure_months + 1 , Python first computes the right side, then moves the label to the new value. Step through it. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [2]: Copied! customer_id = "CM-10482" plan = "Plus" monthly_bill = 31.9 tenure_months = 14 autopay = True print ( customer_id , plan , monthly_bill , tenure_months , autopay ) customer_id = "CM-10482" plan = "Plus" monthly_bill = 31.9 tenure_months = 14 autopay = True print(customer_id, plan, monthly_bill, tenure_months, autopay) CM-10482 Plus 31.9 14 True Every value has a type , and the type decides what you can do with it. You will meet four all the time: type what it holds Cordillera example str text, in quotes "Plus" , "CM-10482" int whole numbers 14 months float numbers with decimals 31.9 USD bool True or False autopay = True In [3]: Copied! print ( type ( plan )) print ( type ( tenure_months )) print ( type ( monthly_bill )) print ( type ( autopay )) print(type(plan)) print(type(tenure_months)) print(type(monthly_bill)) print(type(autopay)) Data often arrives as text: a CSV export or a web form gives you "14" , not 14 . Text and numbers don't mix, so you convert with int() , float() or str() . To write sentences for a report, use an f-string : put an f before the quotes and any variable inside { } . Add :.2f to show two decimals, or :,.2f to also add a thousands separator. In [4]: Copied! tenure_text = "14" # as it came from a web form try : tenure_text + 1 except Exception as e : print ( type ( e ) . __name__ , "→" , e ) print ( int ( tenure_text ) + 1 ) # convert first, then add print ( float ( "31.9" ) * 2 ) print ( "Months: " + str ( tenure_months )) tenure_text = "14" # as it came from a web form try: tenure_text + 1 except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__, "→", e) print(int(tenure_text) + 1) # convert first, then add print(float("31.9") * 2) print("Months: " + str(tenure_months)) TypeError → can only concatenate str (not "int") to str 15 63.8 Months: 14 In [5]: Copied! # f-strings: variables inside { }, formats after a colon print ( f "Customer { customer_id } is on the { plan } plan and has been with us { tenure_months } months." ) print ( f "Last bill: { monthly_bill : .2f } USD. A year at this price: { monthly_bill * 12 : ,.2f } USD." ) # f-strings: variables inside { }, formats after a colon print(f"Customer {customer_id} is on the {plan} plan and has been with us {tenure_months} months.") print(f"Last bill: {monthly_bill:.2f} USD. A year at this price: {monthly_bill * 12:,.2f} USD.") Customer CM-10482 is on the Plus plan and has been with us 14 months. Last bill: 31.90 USD. A year at this price: 382.80 USD. {"q": "A file gives you tenure = \"14\". What is type(tenure)?", "options": ["int, because 14 is a whole number", "str, because it is in quotes", "float"], "answer": 1, "why": "Quotes make it text, whatever it looks like. Use int(tenure) before doing any arithmetic with it.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 Variables and types

docs.text: One bill says little. The commercial team wants to see the trend : the last six monthly bills of CM-10482, April to September. A list keeps many values in order, inside square brackets. Each item has a position, its index , and Python counts from 0 . Negative indices count from the end, so bills[-1] is always the latest bill, however long the list is. A slice bills[start:stop] takes a range and never includes stop . Try some expressions. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [6]: Copied! months = [ "Apr" , "May" , "Jun" , "Jul" , "Aug" , "Sep" ] bills = [ 29.4 , 30.8 , 30.1 , 35.6 , 32.3 , 31.9 ] print ( "First month:" , months [ 0 ], bills [ 0 ]) print ( "Latest month:" , months [ - 1 ], bills [ - 1 ]) print ( "Last three bills:" , bills [ - 3 :]) plans = [ "Prepaid" , "Basic" , "Plus" , "Unlimited" ] # lists can hold text too print ( len ( plans ), "plans; is 'Plus' one of them?" , "Plus" in plans ) months = ["Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep"] bills = [29.4, 30.8, 30.1, 35.6, 32.3, 31.9] print("First month:", months[0], bills[0]) print("Latest month:", months[-1], bills[-1]) print("Last three bills:", bills[-3:]) plans = ["Prepaid", "Basic", "Plus", "Unlimited"] # lists can hold text too print(len(plans), "plans; is 'Plus' one of them?", "Plus" in plans) First month: Apr 29.4 Latest month: Sep 31.9 Last three bills: [35.6, 32.3, 31.9] 4 plans; is 'Plus' one of them? True Lists come with tools that answer business questions in one line: how many items ( len ), the total ( sum ), the extremes ( min , max ). In [7]: Copied! average = sum ( bills ) / len ( bills ) print ( f " { len ( bills ) } bills, { sum ( bills ) : .2f } USD in total" ) print ( f "Average bill: { average : .2f } USD (lowest { min ( bills ) } , highest { max ( bills ) } )" ) print ( "Highest month:" , months [ bills . index ( max ( bills ))]) average = sum(bills) / len(bills) print(f"{len(bills)} bills, {sum(bills):.2f} USD in total") print(f"Average bill: {average:.2f} USD (lowest {min(bills)}, highest {max(bills)})") print("Highest month:", months[bills.index(max(bills))]) 6 bills, 190.10 USD in total Average bill: 31.68 USD (lowest 29.4, highest 35.6) Highest month: Jul The July spike (35.6 USD) is the kind of "bill shock" the retention team worries about. Lists can also grow: append adds an item at the end. October's bill just came in. We rebuild the list inside the cell on purpose: with a plain bills.append(33.0) , every extra run of the cell would add October again (the "cell run twice" trap from the first explainer). In [8]: Copied! october = [ 29.4 , 30.8 , 30.1 , 35.6 , 32.3 , 31.9 ] # a fresh copy of the six bills october . append ( 33.0 ) # add October's bill print ( october , "→" , len ( october ), "bills" ) october = [29.4, 30.8, 30.1, 35.6, 32.3, 31.9] # a fresh copy of the six bills october.append(33.0) # add October's bill print(october, "→", len(october), "bills") [29.4, 30.8, 30.1, 35.6, 32.3, 31.9, 33.0] → 7 bills {"q": "With bills = [29.4, 30.8, 30.1, 35.6, 32.3, 31.9], what does bills[1:3] return?", "options": ["[29.4, 30.8, 30.1]", "[30.8, 30.1]", "[30.8, 30.1, 35.6]"], "answer": 1, "why": "Index 1 is the second bill, and the slice stops before index 3, so you get the items at positions 1 and 2.", "code": false}
docs.title: 03 Lists: a customer's last six bills

docs.text: Five loose variables for one customer gets messy fast. A dictionary ( dict ) keeps all the facts about the customer together, each under a name called a key : customer["plan"] reads like a column name in a spreadsheet row. You look a value up by its key, not by position. Asking for a key that isn't there raises a KeyError ; .get(key, default) returns a default instead. Try both. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [9]: Copied! customer = { "customer_id" : "CM-10482" , "plan" : "Plus" , "contract" : "Month-to-month" , "monthly_bill" : 31.9 , "tenure_months" : 14 , "support_tickets" : 2 , "autopay" : True , } print ( customer [ "plan" ], customer [ "monthly_bill" ]) print ( f " { customer [ 'customer_id' ] } has opened { customer [ 'support_tickets' ] } support tickets." ) customer = { "customer_id": "CM-10482", "plan": "Plus", "contract": "Month-to-month", "monthly_bill": 31.9, "tenure_months": 14, "support_tickets": 2, "autopay": True, } print(customer["plan"], customer["monthly_bill"]) print(f"{customer['customer_id']} has opened {customer['support_tickets']} support tickets.") Plus 31.9 CM-10482 has opened 2 support tickets. October has started, so CM-10482 is one month older as a customer. Assigning to an existing key replaces its value. The CRM has no region for this customer, so we ask for it safely with .get . In [10]: Copied! customer [ "tenure_months" ] = 15 # update the record print ( "Tenure now:" , customer [ "tenure_months" ], "months" ) print ( "Region:" , customer . get ( "region" , "Unknown" )) try : customer [ "region" ] except Exception as e : print ( type ( e ) . __name__ , "→" , e ) print ( len ( customer ), "fields:" , list ( customer . keys ())) customer["tenure_months"] = 15 # update the record print("Tenure now:", customer["tenure_months"], "months") print("Region:", customer.get("region", "Unknown")) try: customer["region"] except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__, "→", e) print(len(customer), "fields:", list(customer.keys())) Tenure now: 15 months Region: Unknown KeyError → 'region' 7 fields: ['customer_id', 'plan', 'contract', 'monthly_bill', 'tenure_months', 'support_tickets', 'autopay'] Now the key idea for the rest of the course: a list of dictionaries is a table . Each dict is a row, each key is a column. Here are five customers from the retention team's watch list. In [11]: Copied! customers = [ { "customer_id" : "CM-10482" , "plan" : "Plus" , "contract" : "Month-to-month" , "monthly_bill" : 31.9 , "support_tickets" : 2 }, { "customer_id" : "CM-10517" , "plan" : "Unlimited" , "contract" : "24 months" , "monthly_bill" : 44.1 , "support_tickets" : 0 }, { "customer_id" : "CM-10533" , "plan" : "Basic" , "contract" : "Month-to-month" , "monthly_bill" : 22.75 , "support_tickets" : 4 }, { "customer_id" : "CM-10561" , "plan" : "Prepaid" , "contract" : "Month-to-month" , "monthly_bill" : 11.2 , "support_tickets" : 3 }, { "customer_id" : "CM-10598" , "plan" : "Plus" , "contract" : "12 months" , "monthly_bill" : 36.4 , "support_tickets" : 1 }, ] print ( len ( customers ), "customers" ) print ( "Row 3:" , customers [ 2 ]) print ( "Plan of row 3:" , customers [ 2 ][ "plan" ]) # row 2 (the third), column "plan" customers = [ {"customer_id": "CM-10482", "plan": "Plus", "contract": "Month-to-month", "monthly_bill": 31.9, "support_tickets": 2}, {"customer_id": "CM-10517", "plan": "Unlimited", "contract": "24 months", "monthly_bill": 44.1, "support_tickets": 0}, {"customer_id": "CM-10533", "plan": "Basic", "contract": "Month-to-month", "monthly_bill": 22.75, "support_tickets": 4}, {"customer_id": "CM-10561", "plan": "Prepaid", "contract": "Month-to-month", "monthly_bill": 11.2, "support_tickets": 3}, {"customer_id": "CM-10598", "plan": "Plus", "contract": "12 months", "monthly_bill": 36.4, "support_tickets": 1}, ] print(len(customers), "customers") print("Row 3:", customers[2]) print("Plan of row 3:", customers[2]["plan"]) # row 2 (the third), column "plan" 5 customers Row 3: {'customer_id': 'CM-10533', 'plan': 'Basic', 'contract': 'Month-to-month', 'monthly_bill': 22.75, 'support_tickets': 4} Plan of row 3: Basic
docs.title: 04 Dictionaries: one customer, one record

docs.text: The retention team has a rule of thumb, written on a whiteboard: at risk if the customer is on a month-to-month contract (free to leave any day) and has 3 or more support tickets; watch if only one of the two is true; ok otherwise. In Python that is if / elif / else . Python checks the conditions from the top and runs only the first branch that is true ; the rest are skipped. Move the controls and watch the path. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Conditions are built from comparisons ( == equal, != different, > , >= , < , <= ), which give True or False , combined with and (both must be true), or (at least one) and not . In [12]: Copied! contract = customer [ "contract" ] support_tickets = customer [ "support_tickets" ] print ( contract == "Month-to-month" ) print ( support_tickets >= 3 ) print ( contract == "Month-to-month" and support_tickets >= 3 ) contract = customer["contract"] support_tickets = customer["support_tickets"] print(contract == "Month-to-month") print(support_tickets >= 3) print(contract == "Month-to-month" and support_tickets >= 3) True False False In [13]: Copied! if contract == "Month-to-month" and support_tickets >= 3 : risk = "at risk" elif contract == "Month-to-month" or support_tickets >= 3 : risk = "watch" else : risk = "ok" print ( customer [ "customer_id" ], "→" , risk ) if contract == "Month-to-month" and support_tickets >= 3: risk = "at risk" elif contract == "Month-to-month" or support_tickets >= 3: risk = "watch" else: risk = "ok" print(customer["customer_id"], "→", risk) CM-10482 → watch CM-10482 is month-to-month but has "only" 2 tickets, so they land on "watch": one more complaint and they would be at risk. Notice the indentation : the 4 spaces tell Python which lines belong to each branch. Now a different customer, on a 12-month contract with one ticket: In [14]: Copied! contract = "12 months" support_tickets = 1 if contract == "Month-to-month" and support_tickets >= 3 : risk = "at risk" elif contract == "Month-to-month" or support_tickets >= 3 : risk = "watch" else : risk = "ok" print ( risk ) contract = "12 months" support_tickets = 1 if contract == "Month-to-month" and support_tickets >= 3: risk = "at risk" elif contract == "Month-to-month" or support_tickets >= 3: risk = "watch" else: risk = "ok" print(risk) ok {"q": "A customer is on a month-to-month contract with 0 support tickets. Which branch runs?", "options": ["if → \"at risk\"", "elif → \"watch\"", "else → \"ok\""], "answer": 1, "why": "The if needs both conditions and only one holds, so Python moves to the elif, which needs just one: month-to-month is enough. The else is never checked.", "code": false}
docs.title: 05 Conditionals: the retention team's first rule

docs.text: We just copied the whole rule to check a second customer; with five thousand customers, copying is not an option. Two numbers are due at Monday's meeting: the commercial team wants the total monthly revenue of the watch list, and the retention team wants how many customers are at risk . A for loop runs the same lines once for each item of a list. The loop variable ( c here) takes each customer in turn, and running totals, called accumulators , pile up. Step through it. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [15]: Copied! total = 0 at_risk = 0 for c in customers : total = total + c [ "monthly_bill" ] if c [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" and c [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 : at_risk = at_risk + 1 print ( total , at_risk ) print ( f "Monthly revenue of the list: { total : .2f } USD. Customers at risk: { at_risk } of { len ( customers ) } ." ) total = 0 at_risk = 0 for c in customers: total = total + c["monthly_bill"] if c["contract"] == "Month-to-month" and c["support_tickets"] >= 3: at_risk = at_risk + 1 print(total, at_risk) print(f"Monthly revenue of the list: {total:.2f} USD. Customers at risk: {at_risk} of {len(customers)}.") 146.35 2 Monthly revenue of the list: 146.35 USD. Customers at risk: 2 of 5. In [16]: Copied! # The same loop, one line per customer: the retention team's call sheet for c in customers : flag = "CALL" if c [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" and c [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 else "" print ( f " { c [ 'customer_id' ] } { c [ 'plan' ] : <10 } { c [ 'monthly_bill' ] : >6.2f } USD { flag } " ) # The same loop, one line per customer: the retention team's call sheet for c in customers: flag = "CALL" if c["contract"] == "Month-to-month" and c["support_tickets"] >= 3 else "" print(f"{c['customer_id']} {c['plan']: < 10} {c['monthly_bill']:>6.2f} USD {flag}") CM-10482 Plus 31.90 USD CM-10517 Unlimited 44.10 USD CM-10533 Basic 22.75 USD CALL CM-10561 Prepaid 11.20 USD CALL CM-10598 Plus 36.40 USD Python also has a compact way to build a list from a loop, the list comprehension . Read [c["monthly_bill"] for c in customers] as "the bill of every c in customers" . Add if ... at the end to keep only some items. Toggle the explainer above to comprehension to watch it happen. In [17]: Copied! monthly_bills = [ c [ "monthly_bill" ] for c in customers ] print ( monthly_bills ) print ( "Total:" , sum ( monthly_bills )) to_call = [ c [ "customer_id" ] for c in customers if c [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" and c [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 ] print ( "Who should we call?" , to_call ) monthly_bills = [c["monthly_bill"] for c in customers] print(monthly_bills) print("Total:", sum(monthly_bills)) to_call = [c["customer_id"] for c in customers if c["contract"] == "Month-to-month" and c["support_tickets"] >= 3] print("Who should we call?", to_call) [31.9, 44.1, 22.75, 11.2, 36.4] Total: 146.35 Who should we call? ['CM-10533', 'CM-10561'] Business takeaway: the loop and the comprehension give the same answer (146.35 USD, 2 customers to call). Use whichever you can read more easily; comprehensions shine for short "take this from every row" jobs.
docs.title: 06 Loops: every customer, one rule

docs.text: We have now typed the retention rule three times. A function packages it under a name: you write it once with def , and call it for any customer. What goes in are the arguments , what comes out is the return value . The commercial team needs a second function: a quick bill estimate from Cordillera's price list (plan base price plus 0.55 USD per GB of data, only 0.10 USD per GB on Unlimited, plus 8 USD for roaming). A parameter can have a default value, used when the caller leaves it out: watch the machine with roaming left out, then tick roaming=True . ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [18]: Copied! def risk_level ( customer ): """Retention rule: 'at risk', 'watch' or 'ok'.""" month_to_month = customer [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" many_tickets = customer [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 if month_to_month and many_tickets : return "at risk" elif month_to_month or many_tickets : return "watch" else : return "ok" for c in customers : print ( c [ "customer_id" ], "→" , risk_level ( c )) def risk_level(customer): """Retention rule: 'at risk', 'watch' or 'ok'.""" month_to_month = customer["contract"] == "Month-to-month" many_tickets = customer["support_tickets"] >= 3 if month_to_month and many_tickets: return "at risk" elif month_to_month or many_tickets: return "watch" else: return "ok" for c in customers: print(c["customer_id"], "→", risk_level(c)) CM-10482 → watch CM-10517 → ok CM-10533 → at risk CM-10561 → at risk CM-10598 → ok In [19]: Copied! def estimate_bill ( plan , data_gb , roaming = False ): base = { "Prepaid" : 9 , "Basic" : 18 , "Plus" : 29 , "Unlimited" : 42 }[ plan ] per_gb = 0.10 if plan == "Unlimited" else 0.55 bill = base + per_gb * data_gb if roaming : bill = bill + 8 return round ( bill , 2 ) estimate = estimate_bill ( "Plus" , 5.2 ) print ( "Plus, 5.2 GB:" , estimate ) print ( "Plus, 5.2 GB, roaming:" , estimate_bill ( "Plus" , 5.2 , roaming = True )) print ( "Unlimited, 30 GB:" , estimate_bill ( "Unlimited" , 30 )) def estimate_bill(plan, data_gb, roaming=False): base = {"Prepaid": 9, "Basic": 18, "Plus": 29, "Unlimited": 42}[plan] per_gb = 0.10 if plan == "Unlimited" else 0.55 bill = base + per_gb * data_gb if roaming: bill = bill + 8 return round(bill, 2) estimate = estimate_bill("Plus", 5.2) print("Plus, 5.2 GB:", estimate) print("Plus, 5.2 GB, roaming:", estimate_bill("Plus", 5.2, roaming=True)) print("Unlimited, 30 GB:", estimate_bill("Unlimited", 30)) Plus, 5.2 GB: 31.86 Plus, 5.2 GB, roaming: 39.86 Unlimited, 30 GB: 45.0 CM-10482 used 5.2 GB last month on Plus, so the price list says about 31.86 USD; the real bill was 31.9. The small gap comes from things the estimate ignores (call minutes, contract discounts). In session 3 you will let the data learn these prices on its own, with a regression model: that is the commercial team's question. Functions combine with comprehensions, too: one line gives the risk level of the whole list. In [20]: Copied! levels = [ risk_level ( c ) for c in customers ] print ( levels ) print ( "At risk:" , levels . count ( "at risk" ), "| watch:" , levels . count ( "watch" ), "| ok:" , levels . count ( "ok" )) levels = [risk_level(c) for c in customers] print(levels) print("At risk:", levels.count("at risk"), "| watch:", levels.count("watch"), "| ok:", levels.count("ok")) ['watch', 'ok', 'at risk', 'at risk', 'ok'] At risk: 2 | watch: 1 | ok: 2 {"q": "What does estimate_bill(\"Basic\", 10) return?", "options": ["18", "23.5", "31.5"], "answer": 1, "why": "Basic costs 18 plus 0.55 × 10 = 5.5 for data. roaming was not passed, so it takes its default False and the 8 USD are not added.", "code": false}
docs.title: 07 Functions: write the rule once

docs.text: Five customers fit in a loop. Cordillera has five thousand , and every month adds five thousand new bills. Python loops handle one item at a time, which gets slow at that scale. NumPy stores numbers in an array and runs an operation on all of them at once, in fast compiled code: bills * 1.05 raises every price in one step, bills > 40 checks every bill in one step. Race the two approaches. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [21]: Copied! import numpy as np bills = np . array ([ 29.4 , 30.8 , 30.1 , 35.6 , 32.3 , 31.9 ]) # CM-10482, April to September print ( bills * 1.05 ) # every bill after a 5% rise, no loop print ( bills . mean (), bills . max ()) print ( bills > 31 ) # which months were above 31 USD? import numpy as np bills = np.array([29.4, 30.8, 30.1, 35.6, 32.3, 31.9]) # CM-10482, April to September print(bills * 1.05) # every bill after a 5% rise, no loop print(bills.mean(), bills.max()) print(bills > 31) # which months were above 31 USD? [30.87 32.34 31.605 37.38 33.915 33.495] 31.683333333333334 35.6 [False False False True True True] Now the real scale. We simulate one month for 5,000 customers with Cordillera's price list (step 09 swaps the simulation for the real file). base_prices[plan_idx] looks up 5,000 base prices at once, and np.where picks the per-GB price for every customer: this is estimate_bill without a loop. In [22]: Copied! rng = np . random . default_rng ( 42 ) n = 5000 plan_idx = rng . choice ( 4 , size = n , p = [ 0.25 , 0.30 , 0.28 , 0.17 ]) # 0 Prepaid, 1 Basic, 2 Plus, 3 Unlimited data_gb = rng . gamma ( 4.0 , 3.0 , size = n ) . round ( 1 ) base_prices = np . array ([ 9 , 18 , 29 , 42 ]) per_gb = np . where ( plan_idx == 3 , 0.10 , 0.55 ) month_bills = ( base_prices [ plan_idx ] + per_gb * data_gb ) . round ( 2 ) print ( month_bills [: 8 ]) print ( f " { len ( month_bills ) : , } bills, monthly revenue { month_bills . sum () : ,.2f } USD, average { month_bills . mean () : .2f } USD" ) rng = np.random.default_rng(42) n = 5000 plan_idx = rng.choice(4, size=n, p=[0.25, 0.30, 0.28, 0.17]) # 0 Prepaid, 1 Basic, 2 Plus, 3 Unlimited data_gb = rng.gamma(4.0, 3.0, size=n).round(1) base_prices = np.array([9, 18, 29, 42]) per_gb = np.where(plan_idx == 3, 0.10, 0.55) month_bills = (base_prices[plan_idx] + per_gb * data_gb).round(2) print(month_bills[:8]) print(f"{len(month_bills):,} bills, monthly revenue {month_bills.sum():,.2f} USD, average {month_bills.mean():.2f} USD") [32.19 24.93 42.95 34.01 21.6 43.93 31.48 32.8 ] 5,000 bills, monthly revenue 142,033.33 USD, average 28.41 USD Business questions become one-liners. What does a 5% price rise bring in? How many customers pay more than 40 USD? A comparison gives a boolean mask , an array of True / False ; sum counts the True s and mean gives their share. In [23]: Copied! extra = ( month_bills * 1.05 ) . sum () - month_bills . sum () print ( f "A 5% rise adds { extra : ,.2f } USD a month" ) high = month_bills > 40 print ( f " { high . sum () : , } customers pay more than 40 USD ( { high . mean () : .1% } of the base)" ) print ( "Their average bill:" , round ( month_bills [ high ] . mean (), 2 )) extra = (month_bills * 1.05).sum() - month_bills.sum() print(f"A 5% rise adds {extra:,.2f} USD a month") high = month_bills > 40 print(f"{high.sum():,} customers pay more than 40 USD ({high.mean():.1%} of the base)") print("Their average bill:", round(month_bills[high].mean(), 2)) A 5% rise adds 7,101.67 USD a month 968 customers pay more than 40 USD (19.4% of the base) Their average bill: 43.13 And the speed? Here is the same estimate done both ways. The exact times depend on your computer, but the gap is always large, and it grows with the data. In [24]: Copied! import time plan_names = np . array ( plans )[ plan_idx ] # 'Prepaid', 'Basic', ... for each customer t0 = time . perf_counter () loop_bills = [ estimate_bill ( p , d ) for p , d in zip ( plan_names , data_gb )] t_loop = time . perf_counter () - t0 t0 = time . perf_counter () array_bills = ( base_prices [ plan_idx ] + per_gb * data_gb ) . round ( 2 ) t_numpy = time . perf_counter () - t0 print ( f "Python loop: { t_loop * 1000 : .1f } ms | NumPy: { t_numpy * 1000 : .2f } ms | about { t_loop / t_numpy : .0f } x faster" ) print ( "Same answers?" , np . allclose ( loop_bills , array_bills )) import time plan_names = np.array(plans)[plan_idx] # 'Prepaid', 'Basic', ... for each customer t0 = time.perf_counter() loop_bills = [estimate_bill(p, d) for p, d in zip(plan_names, data_gb)] t_loop = time.perf_counter() - t0 t0 = time.perf_counter() array_bills = (base_prices[plan_idx] + per_gb * data_gb).round(2) t_numpy = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"Python loop: {t_loop * 1000:.1f} ms | NumPy: {t_numpy * 1000:.2f} ms | about {t_loop / t_numpy:.0f}x faster") print("Same answers?", np.allclose(loop_bills, array_bills)) Python loop: 11.7 ms | NumPy: 0.10 ms | about 115x faster Same answers? True {"q": "What does np.array([20, 35, 50]) > 30 return?", "options": ["True", "array([False, True, True])", "array([35, 50])"], "answer": 1, "why": "The comparison runs on every element and gives one True/False per bill: a mask. To get the bills themselves, use the mask inside brackets: bills[bills > 30].", "code": false}
docs.title: 08 NumPy: thousands of customers at once

docs.text: Time for the real thing. Cordillera's customer base is a CSV file with one row per customer. To read it we use pandas , the library you will use every week from now on. A pandas DataFrame is a table: like our list of dictionaries, but each column is a NumPy array with a name. First, our five customers as a DataFrame: In [25]: Copied! import pandas as pd pd . DataFrame ( customers ) import pandas as pd pd.DataFrame(customers) Out[25]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id plan contract monthly_bill support_tickets 0 CM-10482 Plus Month-to-month 31.90 2 1 CM-10517 Unlimited 24 months 44.10 0 2 CM-10533 Basic Month-to-month 22.75 4 3 CM-10561 Prepaid Month-to-month 11.20 3 4 CM-10598 Plus 12 months 36.40 1 Now the full file. pd.read_csv reads it straight from its URL, so the notebook works for anyone who opens it, with nothing to upload. Before analysing anything, an analyst always runs the same first inspection : size, first rows, column types, missing values and duplicate rows. In [26]: Copied! RAW = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile.csv" df = pd . read_csv ( RAW ) print ( df . shape ) print ( f " { df . shape [ 0 ] : , } rows (customers) and { df . shape [ 1 ] } columns" ) RAW = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile.csv" df = pd.read_csv(RAW) print(df.shape) print(f"{df.shape[0]:,} rows (customers) and {df.shape[1]} columns") (5075, 15) 5,075 rows (customers) and 15 columns In [27]: Copied! df . head () df.head() Out[27]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id signup_date age region plan contract tenure_months data_gb call_minutes intl_roaming support_tickets autopay payment_method monthly_bill churned 0 CM-12254 2022-07-04 34 Metropolitana Basic 12 months 50 NaN 270 0 2 1 NaN 25.46 0 1 CM-10173 2026-06-26 31 Centro Plus 12 months 3 19.0 310 0 0 0 Debit card 37.05 1 2 CM-11339 2020-05-29 38 Centro Prepaid Month-to-month 76 3.6 165 0 0 1 Credit card 11.43 0 3 CM-13440 2019-11-02 31 Centro Unlimited 12 months 82 17.8 248 0 2 0 Debit card 40.97 0 4 CM-10214 2022-07-01 34 Metropolitana Basic Month-to-month 50 4.3 240 0 0 0 Cash 19.18 1 In [28]: Copied! df . dtypes df.dtypes Out[28]: customer_id object signup_date object age int64 region object plan object contract object tenure_months int64 data_gb float64 call_minutes int64 intl_roaming int64 support_tickets int64 autopay int64 payment_method object monthly_bill float64 churned int64 dtype: object Each row is a customer, each column a fact about them. Two columns are the answers our two teams care about: monthly_bill (commercial team) and churned , 1 if the customer cancelled within three months (retention team). In dtypes , int64 and float64 are numbers and object means text. Note that signup_date came in as text, not as a date: worth remembering. Next, the two counts every inspection needs, missing values per column and duplicate rows: In [29]: Copied! print ( "Duplicate rows:" , df . duplicated () . sum ()) df . isna () . sum () print("Duplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum()) df.isna().sum() Duplicate rows: 75 Out[29]: customer_id 0 signup_date 0 age 0 region 0 plan 0 contract 0 tenure_months 0 data_gb 201 call_minutes 0 intl_roaming 0 support_tickets 0 autopay 0 payment_method 154 monthly_bill 0 churned 0 dtype: int64 So: 201 customers without data_gb , 154 without payment_method , and 75 rows that appear twice. Look a little closer and there is more dirt: In [30]: Copied! print ( df [ "region" ] . unique ()) print ( f "Bills go from { df [ 'monthly_bill' ] . min () } to { df [ 'monthly_bill' ] . max () } USD" ) print ( f "Mean bill { df [ 'monthly_bill' ] . mean () : .2f } USD vs median { df [ 'monthly_bill' ] . median () : .2f } USD" ) print(df["region"].unique()) print(f"Bills go from {df['monthly_bill'].min()} to {df['monthly_bill'].max()} USD") print(f"Mean bill {df['monthly_bill'].mean():.2f} USD vs median {df['monthly_bill'].median():.2f} USD") ['Metropolitana' 'Centro' 'Sur' 'Norte' 'Metropolitana ' 'norte' 'Sur ' 'sur' 'metropolitana' 'METROPOLITANA' 'NORTE'] Bills go from -36.08 to 4689.0 USD Mean bill 33.34 USD vs median 29.05 USD "Norte", "NORTE" and "norte" are the same region typed three ways; a bill can't be negative, and nobody pays 4,689 USD a month on a mobile plan. Those few absurd bills are enough to pull the mean above the median. Business takeaway: real data is never clean, and dirt changes the answers. Today we only look ; we don't fix anything yet. Cleaning it, step by step and with each decision justified, is session 2.

Two teams are waiting for answers: the commercial team : what drives a customer's monthly bill? the retention team : which customers are about to cancel, and who should we call? Neither question can be answered with dirty data. A customer stored twice counts twice; one bill of 4,689 USD drags every average. Today you will: look inside a DataFrame and select exactly the rows and columns you need, audit the file and clean it, with a reason for every decision, find the first patterns with groupby and four charts. The retention team's first question: does churn depend on the contract? That is a groupby : split the customers by contract, apply a calculation inside each group, combine the answers into one small table. The rule: start from the question, then pick the chart . one numeric variable, how it spreads → histogram a number compared across categories → box plot a rate per category → bar chart two numbers, do they move together → scatter plot Every chart gets a title, labelled axes, and one sentence under it saying what it shows . It is a number plus what it means for someone . A good template: What we see (with the number) → what it means for the business → what to look at next . First, the numbers we will quote, all in one place: In [32]: Copied! rest_rate = df . loc [ df [ "region" ] != "Norte" , "churned" ] . mean () print ( f "Churn: month-to-month { churn_by_contract [ 'Month-to-month' ] : .1% } , " f "12 months { churn_by_contract [ '12 months' ] : .1% } , 24 months { churn_by_contract [ '24 months' ] : .1% } " ) print ( f "Churn: Norte { churn_by_region [ 'Norte' ] : .1% } , other regions { rest_rate : .1% } " ) print ( f "Call list (month-to-month, 3+ tickets): { len ( call_list ) } customers, churn { call_list [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "Median bill: Prepaid { bill_by_plan . loc [ 'Prepaid' , 'median' ] : .2f } , Unlimited { bill_by_plan . loc [ 'Unlimited' , 'median' ] : .2f } USD" ) print ( f "Correlation data_gb vs monthly_bill: { corr : .2f } " ) rest_rate = df.loc[df["region"] != "Norte", "churned"].mean() print(f"Churn: month-to-month {churn_by_contract['Month-to-month']:.1%}, " f"12 months {churn_by_contract['12 months']:.1%}, 24 months {churn_by_contract['24 months']:.1%}") print(f"Churn: Norte {churn_by_region['Norte']:.1%}, other regions {rest_rate:.1%}") print(f"Call list (month-to-month, 3+ tickets): {len(call_list)} customers, churn {call_list['churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"Median bill: Prepaid {bill_by_plan.loc['Prepaid', 'median']:.2f}, Unlimited {bill_by_plan.loc['Unlimited', 'median']:.2f} USD") print(f"Correlation data_gb vs monthly_bill: {corr:.2f}") Churn: month-to-month 22.0%, 12 months 8.9%, 24 months 7.8% Churn: Norte 27.6%, other regions 14.3% Call list (month-to-month, 3+ tickets): 147 customers, churn 68.7% Median bill: Prepaid 14.28, Unlimited 46.44 USD Correlation data_gb vs monthly_bill: 0.75 Finding 1 · Contracts keep customers. Month-to-month customers churn at 22.0%, against 7.8% on 24-month contracts: almost three times as often. For the retention team: moving month-to-month customers onto a contract is the biggest lever we have seen so far; a small discount for switching is worth testing. Next: does the gap hold within every plan? Finding 2 · Complaints come before cancellations, especially in the north. Norte churns at 27.6%, against 14.3% in the other regions, and month-to-month customers with 3 or more tickets churn at 68.7%. For the retention team: those 147 customers are the first call list, and Norte's complaints deserve a conversation with the network team. Next: what are Norte's tickets about? Finding 3 · The plan sets the bill; data use moves it within the plan. The median bill goes from 14.28 USD on Prepaid to 46.44 USD on Unlimited, and data use correlates 0.75 with the bill. For the commercial team: to explain a bill, start from the plan and the gigabytes. Next: how many dollars does each extra GB add, once the plan is taken into account? That needs a model, and it is session 3. Notice what these findings are not : they are not proof that a contract causes customers to stay. Customers who sign 24 months may simply be happier to begin with. Findings point where to look; models and experiments come later. 10 Your project this week ¶ Advance 2 · Cleaning and exploratory analysis is due Tuesday, November 10, 23:59 . It is today's class, done on your team's data. We did it with monthly_bill and churned ; you do it with Salary (Case A) or default (Case B). Justify each decision in one line. "We dropped them" is not a justification; "a bill is our target and we cannot know the true value" is. At least one chart must relate a variable to the target : that is the point of the exploration. Run Restart session and run all before you submit. The notebook must run top to bottom. docs.text: Last week you joined the analytics team, loaded cordillera_mobile.csv and took a first look: 5,075 rows, 15 columns, some missing values and some duplicate rows. Two teams are waiting for answers: the commercial team : what drives a customer's monthly bill? the retention team : which customers are about to cancel, and who should we call? Neither question can be answered with dirty data. A customer stored twice counts twice; one bill of 4,689 USD drags every average. Today you will: look inside a DataFrame and select exactly the rows and columns you need, audit the file and clean it, with a reason for every decision, find the first patterns with groupby and four charts. That is exactly what Advance 2 asks of your team. docs.text: Before you clean anything, know what you are holding. raw is a DataFrame : a table with rows , one per customer, labelled by the index (0, 1, 2… by default), columns , one per variable, each with a dtype : object for text, int64 for whole numbers, float64 for decimals, values , the data itself. Take out one column and you get a Series : one variable for every customer, with the index still attached. Three methods are your first look at any new table: head() shows the first rows, info() lists the columns with their dtypes and non-missing counts, and describe() summarises the numeric columns. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. docs.text: Most questions start by narrowing the table: only these columns , only that customer . Square brackets pick columns by name: raw["plan"] gives a Series, raw[["plan", "monthly_bill"]] (double brackets) a DataFrame. For rows, pandas has two tools, and mixing them up is the classic beginner bug: .loc[rows, columns] selects by label : the names in the index and the column names. A slice includes its stop. .iloc[rows, columns] selects by position : 0, 1, 2… like a Python list. A slice excludes its stop. With the default index (0, 1, 2…) labels and positions look the same. Make customer_id the index and they part ways. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. docs.text: The retention team's first request: month-to-month customers with 3 or more support tickets . They can leave any day, and they are unhappy. A comparison on a column, like raw["contract"] == "Month-to-month" , gives a boolean mask : a Series of True/False, one per customer. Put the mask inside raw[...] and only the True rows survive. Combine masks with & (and), | (or) and ~ (not), with each condition in its own parentheses . Two helpers save typing: isin([...]) for "one of these values" and between(a, b) for a range, both ends included. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [9]: Copied! m2m = raw [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" print ( m2m . head ()) # True counts as 1 and False as 0: sum() counts the Trues, mean() gives their share print ( f " { m2m . sum () : , } customers are month-to-month ( { m2m . mean () : .1% } )" ) m2m = raw["contract"] == "Month-to-month" print(m2m.head()) # True counts as 1 and False as 0: sum() counts the Trues, mean() gives their share print(f"{m2m.sum():,} customers are month-to-month ({m2m.mean():.1%})") 0 False 1 False 2 True 3 False 4 True Name: contract, dtype: bool 2,979 customers are month-to-month (58.7%) In [10]: Copied! many_tickets = raw [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 call_list = raw [ m2m & many_tickets ] print ( f "Month-to-month with 3+ tickets: { len ( call_list ) } customers" ) print ( f "Their churn rate: { call_list [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } , against { raw [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } overall" ) # still the raw file, duplicates included: we recount this list after cleaning many_tickets = raw["support_tickets"] >= 3 call_list = raw[m2m & many_tickets] print(f"Month-to-month with 3+ tickets: {len(call_list)} customers") print(f"Their churn rate: {call_list['churned'].mean():.1%}, against {raw['churned'].mean():.1%} overall") # still the raw file, duplicates included: we recount this list after cleaning Month-to-month with 3+ tickets: 151 customers Their churn rate: 68.2%, against 16.5% overall In [11]: Copied! young = raw [ "age" ] . between ( 18 , 24 ) big_plan = raw [ "plan" ] . isin ([ "Plus" , "Unlimited" ]) print ( f "Aged 18 to 24: { young . sum () : , } " ) print ( f "On Plus or Unlimited: { big_plan . sum () : , } " ) print ( f "...ignoring upper/lower case: { raw [ 'plan' ] . str . lower () . isin ([ 'plus' , 'unlimited' ]) . sum () : , } " ) young = raw["age"].between(18, 24) big_plan = raw["plan"].isin(["Plus", "Unlimited"]) print(f"Aged 18 to 24: {young.sum():,}") print(f"On Plus or Unlimited: {big_plan.sum():,}") print(f"...ignoring upper/lower case: {raw['plan'].str.lower().isin(['plus', 'unlimited']).sum():,}") Aged 18 to 24: 682 On Plus or Unlimited: 2,186 ...ignoring upper/lower case: 2,309 The two plan counts differ: isin compares text exactly, so "PLUS" and "unlimited" slip through. The data is lying to our filters, and that is the next section. First, the most common filtering error. Python applies & before == and >= , so without parentheses it tries to compute "Month-to-month" & raw["support_tickets"] , which makes no sense. Parentheses around each condition fix it. (Writing and instead of & fails too: and wants a single True or False, not a whole column of them.) In [12]: Copied! try : raw [ raw [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" & raw [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 ] # no parentheses except Exception as e : print ( type ( e ) . __name__ , "→" , e ) fixed = raw [( raw [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" ) & ( raw [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 )] print ( f "With parentheses: { len ( fixed ) } rows" ) try: raw[raw["contract"] == "Month-to-month" & raw["support_tickets"] >= 3] # no parentheses except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__, "→", e) fixed = raw[(raw["contract"] == "Month-to-month") & (raw["support_tickets"] >= 3)] print(f"With parentheses: {len(fixed)} rows") TypeError → Cannot perform 'rand_' with a dtyped [int64] array and scalar of type [bool] With parentheses: 151 rows {"q": "What does (df['contract'] == 'Month-to-month') & (df['support_tickets'] >= 3) return?", "options": ["The rows that meet both conditions", "A True/False Series, True only where both conditions are True", "A single True or False", "A True/False Series, True where at least one condition is True"], "answer": 1, "why": "Combining two masks with & gives another mask, row by row. Only df[mask] turns it into rows. True where at least one holds is |.", "code": false}
docs.title: 04 Filtering with conditions

docs.text: Now point those tools at the data itself. An audit asks one question per kind of problem, answers it with code, and writes down the count: Are there duplicate rows ? Are categories spelled consistently ? Are there impossible values (ages, bills)? What is missing ? Run every check on the raw file before changing anything, so you know what you are about to fix. The explainer runs the whole pipeline at once; the cells below do the audit, and section 06 does the cleaning. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [13]: Copied! # Check 1: duplicates print ( f "Exact duplicate rows: { raw . duplicated () . sum () } " ) raw [ raw . duplicated ( keep = False )] . sort_values ( "customer_id" ) . head ( 4 ) # Check 1: duplicates print(f"Exact duplicate rows: {raw.duplicated().sum()}") raw[raw.duplicated(keep=False)].sort_values("customer_id").head(4) Exact duplicate rows: 75 Out[13]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id signup_date age region plan contract tenure_months data_gb call_minutes intl_roaming support_tickets autopay payment_method monthly_bill churned 1894 CM-10277 2020-01-31 45 Sur Prepaid Month-to-month 79 2.4 201 1 0 1 Debit card 15.65 0 3098 CM-10277 2020-01-31 45 Sur Prepaid Month-to-month 79 2.4 201 1 0 1 Debit card 15.65 0 2744 CM-10340 2021-10-24 35 Metropolitana Unlimited 12 months 59 21.1 457 0 1 1 Bank transfer 46.51 0 1853 CM-10340 2021-10-24 35 Metropolitana Unlimited 12 months 59 21.1 457 0 1 1 Bank transfer 46.51 0 duplicated() marks a row that is identical, column by column, to an earlier one; keep=False marks both copies so you can see the pairs. Check 2, categories: value_counts() lists every distinct text and how often it appears. In [14]: Copied! print ( raw [ "region" ] . value_counts ()) print () print ( "Spellings of region:" , raw [ "region" ] . nunique ()) print ( "Spellings of plan: " , raw [ "plan" ] . nunique ()) print ( raw [ "region" ] . unique ()) print(raw["region"].value_counts()) print() print("Spellings of region:", raw["region"].nunique()) print("Spellings of plan: ", raw["plan"].nunique()) print(raw["region"].unique()) region Metropolitana 2149 Centro 991 Sur 975 Norte 723 Metropolitana 45 metropolitana 43 norte 38 METROPOLITANA 33 NORTE 28 sur 27 Sur 23 Name: count, dtype: int64 Spellings of region: 11 Spellings of plan: 10 ['Metropolitana' 'Centro' 'Sur' 'Norte' 'Metropolitana ' 'norte' 'Sur ' 'sur' 'metropolitana' 'METROPOLITANA' 'NORTE'] There are 4 regions and 4 plans, but pandas sees 11 and 10. unique() shows the quotes, which reveals the sneakiest ones: 'Sur ' and 'Metropolitana ' end with a space. A groupby("region") on this column would report 11 regions. Check 3, impossible values: an age must be between 18 and 100, and a bill between 0 and 300 USD (the most expensive plan costs 42 USD before extras). In [15]: Copied! # Check 3: impossible values bad_age = ~ raw [ "age" ] . between ( 18 , 100 ) print ( f "Ages outside 18-100: { bad_age . sum () } " ) print ( raw . loc [ bad_age , "age" ] . value_counts ()) print () negative = raw [ "monthly_bill" ] < 0 huge = raw [ "monthly_bill" ] > 300 print ( f "Negative bills: { negative . sum () } Bills above 300 USD: { huge . sum () } " ) raw . loc [ huge , [ "customer_id" , "plan" , "monthly_bill" ]] # Check 3: impossible values bad_age = ~raw["age"].between(18, 100) print(f"Ages outside 18-100: {bad_age.sum()}") print(raw.loc[bad_age, "age"].value_counts()) print() negative = raw["monthly_bill"] < 0 huge = raw["monthly_bill"] > 300 print(f"Negative bills: {negative.sum()} Bills above 300 USD: {huge.sum()}") raw.loc[huge, ["customer_id", "plan", "monthly_bill"]] Ages outside 18-100: 15 age 0 7 999 4 -1 4 Name: count, dtype: int64 Negative bills: 10 Bills above 300 USD: 5 Out[15]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id plan monthly_bill 152 CM-10319 Prepaid 1386.0 832 CM-11287 Plus 4119.0 2270 CM-11620 Plus 3458.0 2542 CM-12112 PLUS 4689.0 4093 CM-10247 Basic 2804.0 No plan costs thousands of dollars a month. These look like a lost decimal point: 4,689.00 on a Plus plan is almost surely 46.89. Negative bills could be refunds or typos; the file does not tell us which. Check 4, missing values, goes straight into the audit table, with all the other counts: In [16]: Copied! REGIONS = [ "Metropolitana" , "Centro" , "Sur" , "Norte" ] PLANS = [ "Prepaid" , "Basic" , "Plus" , "Unlimited" ] audit = pd . Series ({ "Duplicate rows" : raw . duplicated () . sum (), "Non-standard region" : ( ~ raw [ "region" ] . isin ( REGIONS )) . sum (), "Non-standard plan" : ( ~ raw [ "plan" ] . isin ( PLANS )) . sum (), "Age outside 18-100" : bad_age . sum (), "Missing data_gb" : raw [ "data_gb" ] . isna () . sum (), "Missing payment_method" : raw [ "payment_method" ] . isna () . sum (), "Bill below 0 or above 300" : ( negative | huge ) . sum (), }, name = "count" ) # raw.isna().sum() would list the missing values of every column print ( audit ) print ( f " \n Dirty values found: { audit . sum () } " ) REGIONS = ["Metropolitana", "Centro", "Sur", "Norte"] PLANS = ["Prepaid", "Basic", "Plus", "Unlimited"] audit = pd.Series({ "Duplicate rows": raw.duplicated().sum(), "Non-standard region": (~raw["region"].isin(REGIONS)).sum(), "Non-standard plan": (~raw["plan"].isin(PLANS)).sum(), "Age outside 18-100": bad_age.sum(), "Missing data_gb": raw["data_gb"].isna().sum(), "Missing payment_method": raw["payment_method"].isna().sum(), "Bill below 0 or above 300": (negative | huge).sum(), }, name="count") # raw.isna().sum() would list the missing values of every column print(audit) print(f"\nDirty values found: {audit.sum()}") Duplicate rows 75 Non-standard region 237 Non-standard plan 228 Age outside 18-100 15 Missing data_gb 201 Missing payment_method 154 Bill below 0 or above 300 15 Name: count, dtype: int64 Dirty values found: 925
docs.title: 05 The data quality audit

docs.text: Every problem needs a decision , and every decision needs a reason a manager would accept: Issue Decision Why Exact duplicates Drop the copies A customer counted twice weighs double in every average Inconsistent spelling strip() + title() Same region, same plan → same text Age outside 18–100 Make it missing, then fill with the median The true age is unknowable; the median ignores extremes Missing data_gb Median of the customer's plan Data use depends strongly on the plan Missing payment_method New category "Unknown" Honest; we don't invent a payment method Bill below 0 or above 300 Drop the row It is the commercial team's target: guessing it would invent the answer Order matters. Drop duplicates first, so copies don't count twice in the medians. Fix the spelling before using plan for group medians. As you go, write each decision into a log: at the end, the log is the cleaning summary table of Advance 2. In [17]: Copied! df = raw . copy () log = [] # one entry per decision: this becomes the cleaning summary table def record ( issue , decision , rows ): log . append ({ "issue" : issue , "decision" : decision , "rows affected" : int ( rows )}) print ( f " { issue } : { rows : , } rows → { decision } " ) # 1. Duplicates before = len ( df ) df = df . drop_duplicates () record ( "Exact duplicate rows" , "Dropped, kept the first copy" , before - len ( df )) df = raw.copy() log = [] # one entry per decision: this becomes the cleaning summary table def record(issue, decision, rows): log.append({"issue": issue, "decision": decision, "rows affected": int(rows)}) print(f"{issue}: {rows:,} rows → {decision}") # 1. Duplicates before = len(df) df = df.drop_duplicates() record("Exact duplicate rows", "Dropped, kept the first copy", before - len(df)) Exact duplicate rows: 75 rows → Dropped, kept the first copy In [18]: Copied! # 2. Spelling: strip spaces at both ends, then Title Case for col in [ "region" , "plan" ]: tidy = df [ col ] . str . strip () . str . title () changed = ( tidy != df [ col ]) . sum () df [ col ] = tidy record ( f "Inconsistent spelling in { col } " , "strip() + title()" , changed ) print ( df [ "region" ] . value_counts ()) # 2. Spelling: strip spaces at both ends, then Title Case for col in ["region", "plan"]: tidy = df[col].str.strip().str.title() changed = (tidy != df[col]).sum() df[col] = tidy record(f"Inconsistent spelling in {col}", "strip() + title()", changed) print(df["region"].value_counts()) Inconsistent spelling in region: 236 rows → strip() + title() Inconsistent spelling in plan: 227 rows → strip() + title() region Metropolitana 2228 Sur 1008 Centro 979 Norte 785 Name: count, dtype: int64 In [19]: Copied! # 3. Impossible ages: unknown → missing → median bad_age = ~ df [ "age" ] . between ( 18 , 100 ) df . loc [ bad_age , "age" ] = np . nan median_age = df [ "age" ] . median () df [ "age" ] = df [ "age" ] . fillna ( median_age ) . astype ( "int64" ) # whole years again record ( "Impossible age (outside 18-100)" , f "Set to NaN, filled with the median ( { median_age : .0f } )" , bad_age . sum ()) # 3. Impossible ages: unknown → missing → median bad_age = ~df["age"].between(18, 100) df.loc[bad_age, "age"] = np.nan median_age = df["age"].median() df["age"] = df["age"].fillna(median_age).astype("int64") # whole years again record("Impossible age (outside 18-100)", f"Set to NaN, filled with the median ({median_age:.0f})", bad_age.sum()) Impossible age (outside 18-100): 15 rows → Set to NaN, filled with the median (38) For data_gb we want the median of each plan : a Prepaid customer uses far less data than an Unlimited one, so one overall median would be wrong for both. groupby is section 07; here read it as "one median per plan". transform("median") puts each row's own plan median next to it, so fillna can use it. In [20]: Copied! # 4. Missing values print ( df . groupby ( "plan" )[ "data_gb" ] . median (), " \n " ) n_gb = df [ "data_gb" ] . isna () . sum () plan_median = df . groupby ( "plan" )[ "data_gb" ] . transform ( "median" ) df [ "data_gb" ] = df [ "data_gb" ] . fillna ( plan_median ) record ( "Missing data_gb" , "Filled with the median of the customer's plan" , n_gb ) n_pay = df [ "payment_method" ] . isna () . sum () df [ "payment_method" ] = df [ "payment_method" ] . fillna ( "Unknown" ) record ( "Missing payment_method" , 'New category "Unknown"' , n_pay ) # 4. Missing values print(df.groupby("plan")["data_gb"].median(), "\n") n_gb = df["data_gb"].isna().sum() plan_median = df.groupby("plan")["data_gb"].transform("median") df["data_gb"] = df["data_gb"].fillna(plan_median) record("Missing data_gb", "Filled with the median of the customer's plan", n_gb) n_pay = df["payment_method"].isna().sum() df["payment_method"] = df["payment_method"].fillna("Unknown") record("Missing payment_method", 'New category "Unknown"', n_pay) plan Basic 7.1 Plus 14.1 Prepaid 3.7 Unlimited 27.5 Name: data_gb, dtype: float64 Missing data_gb: 200 rows → Filled with the median of the customer's plan Missing payment_method: 150 rows → New category "Unknown" In [21]: Copied! # 5. Impossible bills: drop the row bad_bill = ~ df [ "monthly_bill" ] . between ( 0 , 300 ) df = df [ ~ bad_bill ] . reset_index ( drop = True ) record ( "Impossible bill (below 0 or above 300 USD)" , "Dropped the row" , bad_bill . sum ()) # 5. Impossible bills: drop the row bad_bill = ~df["monthly_bill"].between(0, 300) df = df[~bad_bill].reset_index(drop=True) record("Impossible bill (below 0 or above 300 USD)", "Dropped the row", bad_bill.sum()) Impossible bill (below 0 or above 300 USD): 15 rows → Dropped the row In [22]: Copied! # The log becomes the table your manager (and Advance 2) wants to see print ( f "Rows: { len ( raw ) : , } → { len ( df ) : , } ( { len ( raw ) - len ( df ) } removed)" ) print ( f "Missing values left: { df . isna () . sum () . sum () } " ) assert df . shape == ( 4985 , 15 ) summary = pd . DataFrame ( log ) summary # The log becomes the table your manager (and Advance 2) wants to see print(f"Rows: {len(raw):,} → {len(df):,} ({len(raw) - len(df)} removed)") print(f"Missing values left: {df.isna().sum().sum()}") assert df.shape == (4985, 15) summary = pd.DataFrame(log) summary Rows: 5,075 → 4,985 (90 removed) Missing values left: 0 Out[22]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } issue decision rows affected 0 Exact duplicate rows Dropped, kept the first copy 75 1 Inconsistent spelling in region strip() + title() 236 2 Inconsistent spelling in plan strip() + title() 227 3 Impossible age (outside 18-100) Set to NaN, filled with the median (38) 15 4 Missing data_gb Filled with the median of the customer's plan 200 5 Missing payment_method New category "Unknown" 150 6 Impossible bill (below 0 or above 300 USD) Dropped the row 15 Last check: does our cleaning give exactly the clean file that sessions 3 to 5 start from? assert_frame_equal compares every value and every dtype, and raises an error at the first difference. In [23]: Copied! published = pd . read_csv ( CLEAN ) pd . testing . assert_frame_equal ( df , published ) print ( "Matches the published clean file" ) published = pd.read_csv(CLEAN) pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(df, published) print("Matches the published clean file") Matches the published clean file {"q": "Why do we fill a missing data_gb with the median of the customer's plan instead of the overall median?", "options": ["Because the overall median cannot be computed while there are missing values", "Because data use depends strongly on the plan, so the plan's median is a much closer guess", "Because pandas requires groupby before fillna", "Because it removes the outliers"], "answer": 1, "why": "A Prepaid customer uses about 3.7 GB and an Unlimited one about 27.5 GB. One overall number would be wrong for both. The more the guess uses what we know about the customer, the less it distorts the data.", "code": false}
docs.title: 06 Cleaning, with decisions you can defend

docs.text: Clean data at last. The retention team's first question: does churn depend on the contract? That is a groupby : split the customers by contract, apply a calculation inside each group, combine the answers into one small table. Because churned is 0/1, its mean in a group is the share of customers who left: the churn rate . The explainer uses a toy example (stock prices) because the three moves are easier to watch on nine rows. Right after it, the same moves on our 4,985 customers. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [24]: Copied! print ( f "Overall churn rate: { df [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } \n " ) churn_by_contract = df . groupby ( "contract" )[ "churned" ] . mean () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) for contract , rate in churn_by_contract . items (): print ( f " { contract : <15 } { rate : .1% } " ) print () churn_by_region = df . groupby ( "region" )[ "churned" ] . mean () . sort_values ( ascending = False ) for region , rate in churn_by_region . items (): print ( f " { region : <14 } { rate : .1% } " ) print(f"Overall churn rate: {df['churned'].mean():.1%}\n") churn_by_contract = df.groupby("contract")["churned"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) for contract, rate in churn_by_contract.items(): print(f"{contract: < 15} {rate:.1%}") print() churn_by_region = df.groupby("region")["churned"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False) for region, rate in churn_by_region.items(): print(f"{region: < 14} {rate:.1%}") Overall churn rate: 16.4% Month-to-month 22.0% 12 months 8.9% 24 months 7.8% Norte 27.6% Metropolitana 15.4% Sur 13.9% Centro 12.4% In [25]: Copied! # Several numbers per group: agg takes a list. For the commercial team, the bill by plan. bill_by_plan = df . groupby ( "plan" )[ "monthly_bill" ] . agg ([ "count" , "mean" , "median" ]) . round ( 2 ) bill_by_plan . sort_values ( "mean" ) # Several numbers per group: agg takes a list. For the commercial team, the bill by plan. bill_by_plan = df.groupby("plan")["monthly_bill"].agg(["count", "mean", "median"]).round(2) bill_by_plan.sort_values("mean") Out[25]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } count mean median plan Prepaid 1193 14.79 14.28 Basic 1504 24.32 23.90 Plus 1438 39.29 39.03 Unlimited 850 46.95 46.44 In [26]: Copied! churn_by_tickets = df . groupby ( "support_tickets" )[ "churned" ] . agg ([ "count" , "mean" ]) . round ( 3 ) churn_by_tickets churn_by_tickets = df.groupby("support_tickets")["churned"].agg(["count", "mean"]).round(3) churn_by_tickets Out[26]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } count mean support_tickets 0 2282 0.128 1 1746 0.138 2 688 0.218 3 208 0.524 4 54 0.426 5 5 0.200 6 2 0.500 Churn jumps at 3 tickets. (The rows with 5 or 6 tickets hold only a handful of customers: never trust a rate built on 2 people.) Now the retention team's call list, recounted on clean data: In [27]: Copied! call_list = df [( df [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" ) & ( df [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 )] print ( f "Call list: { len ( call_list ) } customers, churn rate { call_list [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) call_list = df[(df["contract"] == "Month-to-month") & (df["support_tickets"] >= 3)] print(f"Call list: {len(call_list)} customers, churn rate {call_list['churned'].mean():.1%}") Call list: 147 customers, churn rate 68.7%
docs.title: 07 groupby: the first patterns

docs.text: A table of numbers convinces an analyst; a chart convinces a meeting. The rule: start from the question, then pick the chart . one numeric variable, how it spreads → histogram a number compared across categories → box plot a rate per category → bar chart two numbers, do they move together → scatter plot Every chart gets a title, labelled axes, and one sentence under it saying what it shows . Advance 2 asks for exactly that. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [28]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) sns . histplot ( df , x = "monthly_bill" , bins = 40 ) plt . title ( "How is the monthly bill distributed?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Monthly bill (USD)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Customers" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) sns.histplot(df, x="monthly_bill", bins=40) plt.title("How is the monthly bill distributed?") plt.xlabel("Monthly bill (USD)") plt.ylabel("Customers") plt.show() What it shows: bills run from about 4 to 61 USD with two humps , one around 20–25 USD and one around 40–45 USD. Two humps usually mean two kinds of customers mixed together: here, the cheaper plans and the more expensive ones. No single "typical bill" describes this base. In [29]: Copied! plan_order = [ "Prepaid" , "Basic" , "Plus" , "Unlimited" ] plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) sns . boxplot ( df , x = "plan" , y = "monthly_bill" , order = plan_order ) plt . title ( "Does the bill differ by plan?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Plan" ) plt . ylabel ( "Monthly bill (USD)" ) plt . show () plan_order = ["Prepaid", "Basic", "Plus", "Unlimited"] plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) sns.boxplot(df, x="plan", y="monthly_bill", order=plan_order) plt.title("Does the bill differ by plan?") plt.xlabel("Plan") plt.ylabel("Monthly bill (USD)") plt.show() What it shows: the plan sets the level of the bill. Medians climb from 14.28 USD on Prepaid to 46.44 USD on Unlimited, and neighbouring boxes barely overlap. The dots beyond the whiskers are unusually high bills within a plan: worth a look, but possible, unlike the ones we removed. In [30]: Copied! contract_order = [ "Month-to-month" , "12 months" , "24 months" ] plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax = sns . barplot ( df , x = "contract" , y = "churned" , order = contract_order , errorbar = None ) ax . bar_label ( ax . containers [ 0 ], fmt = " {:.1%} " ) ax . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( PercentFormatter ( 1 )) plt . title ( "Is churn higher on month-to-month?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Contract" ) plt . ylabel ( "Churn rate" ) plt . show () contract_order = ["Month-to-month", "12 months", "24 months"] plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) ax = sns.barplot(df, x="contract", y="churned", order=contract_order, errorbar=None) ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], fmt="{:.1%}") ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PercentFormatter(1)) plt.title("Is churn higher on month-to-month?") plt.xlabel("Contract") plt.ylabel("Churn rate") plt.show() What it shows: 22.0% of month-to-month customers churned, against 8.9% on 12-month and 7.8% on 24-month contracts. Customers without a contract leave almost three times as often as those on a 24-month one. In [31]: Copied! corr = df [ "data_gb" ] . corr ( df [ "monthly_bill" ]) print ( f "Correlation between data_gb and monthly_bill: { corr : .2f } " ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4.5 )) sns . scatterplot ( df , x = "data_gb" , y = "monthly_bill" , hue = "plan" , hue_order = plan_order , alpha = 0.5 , s = 14 ) plt . title ( "Does data usage drive the bill?" ) plt . xlabel ( "Data used last month (GB)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Monthly bill (USD)" ) plt . show () corr = df["data_gb"].corr(df["monthly_bill"]) print(f"Correlation between data_gb and monthly_bill: {corr:.2f}") plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4.5)) sns.scatterplot(df, x="data_gb", y="monthly_bill", hue="plan", hue_order=plan_order, alpha=0.5, s=14) plt.title("Does data usage drive the bill?") plt.xlabel("Data used last month (GB)") plt.ylabel("Monthly bill (USD)") plt.show() Correlation between data_gb and monthly_bill: 0.75 What it shows: more data, higher bill (correlation 0.75). Each plan forms its own band that rises with data, except Unlimited, which is almost flat: extra gigabytes cost those customers almost nothing. Data use matters, but within a plan. {"q": "The retention team asks: is churn higher in the Norte region than elsewhere? Which chart answers it best?", "options": ["A histogram of churned", "A scatter plot of region against churned", "A bar chart of the churn rate (mean of churned) by region", "A box plot of churned by region"], "answer": 2, "why": "The question is a rate per category, so one bar per region, with height = share who churned. A 0/1 column makes histograms and box plots nearly empty, and a scatter of a category against 0/1 is just four stacks of dots.", "code": false}
docs.title: 08 Charts that answer questions

docs.text: A finding is not a number. It is a number plus what it means for someone . A good template: What we see (with the number) → what it means for the business → what to look at next . First, the numbers we will quote, all in one place: In [32]: Copied! rest_rate = df . loc [ df [ "region" ] != "Norte" , "churned" ] . mean () print ( f "Churn: month-to-month { churn_by_contract [ 'Month-to-month' ] : .1% } , " f "12 months { churn_by_contract [ '12 months' ] : .1% } , 24 months { churn_by_contract [ '24 months' ] : .1% } " ) print ( f "Churn: Norte { churn_by_region [ 'Norte' ] : .1% } , other regions { rest_rate : .1% } " ) print ( f "Call list (month-to-month, 3+ tickets): { len ( call_list ) } customers, churn { call_list [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "Median bill: Prepaid { bill_by_plan . loc [ 'Prepaid' , 'median' ] : .2f } , Unlimited { bill_by_plan . loc [ 'Unlimited' , 'median' ] : .2f } USD" ) print ( f "Correlation data_gb vs monthly_bill: { corr : .2f } " ) rest_rate = df.loc[df["region"] != "Norte", "churned"].mean() print(f"Churn: month-to-month {churn_by_contract['Month-to-month']:.1%}, " f"12 months {churn_by_contract['12 months']:.1%}, 24 months {churn_by_contract['24 months']:.1%}") print(f"Churn: Norte {churn_by_region['Norte']:.1%}, other regions {rest_rate:.1%}") print(f"Call list (month-to-month, 3+ tickets): {len(call_list)} customers, churn {call_list['churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"Median bill: Prepaid {bill_by_plan.loc['Prepaid', 'median']:.2f}, Unlimited {bill_by_plan.loc['Unlimited', 'median']:.2f} USD") print(f"Correlation data_gb vs monthly_bill: {corr:.2f}") Churn: month-to-month 22.0%, 12 months 8.9%, 24 months 7.8% Churn: Norte 27.6%, other regions 14.3% Call list (month-to-month, 3+ tickets): 147 customers, churn 68.7% Median bill: Prepaid 14.28, Unlimited 46.44 USD Correlation data_gb vs monthly_bill: 0.75 Finding 1 · Contracts keep customers. Month-to-month customers churn at 22.0%, against 7.8% on 24-month contracts: almost three times as often. For the retention team: moving month-to-month customers onto a contract is the biggest lever we have seen so far; a small discount for switching is worth testing. Next: does the gap hold within every plan? Finding 2 · Complaints come before cancellations, especially in the north. Norte churns at 27.6%, against 14.3% in the other regions, and month-to-month customers with 3 or more tickets churn at 68.7%. For the retention team: those 147 customers are the first call list, and Norte's complaints deserve a conversation with the network team. Next: what are Norte's tickets about? Finding 3 · The plan sets the bill; data use moves it within the plan. The median bill goes from 14.28 USD on Prepaid to 46.44 USD on Unlimited, and data use correlates 0.75 with the bill. For the commercial team: to explain a bill, start from the plan and the gigabytes. Next: how many dollars does each extra GB add, once the plan is taken into account? That needs a model, and it is session 3. Notice what these findings are not : they are not proof that a contract causes customers to stay. Customers who sign 24 months may simply be happier to begin with. Findings point where to look; models and experiments come later.

docs.text: Advance 2 · Cleaning and exploratory analysis is due Tuesday, November 10, 23:59 . It is today's class, done on your team's data. We did it with monthly_bill and churned ; you do it with Salary (Case A) or default (Case B). Today with Cordillera Case A · TalentCo ( Salary ) Case B · FinTrust ( default ) Audit: duplicated() , value_counts() on every text column, describe() , isna().sum() Check the spellings of Education_Level , Department , Region , Job_Level ; look for impossible Age , Years_Experience or a Performance_Score outside 1.0–5.0 Check the spellings of employment_type , loan_purpose , region ; look for a credit_score outside 300–850, a debt_to_income_ratio outside 0–1, impossible ages One decision per issue, logged as you clean Same log + record() pattern Same log + record() pattern Cleaning summary table: issue · decision · rows affected pd.DataFrame(log) pd.DataFrame(log) groupby on the target Average Salary by department, education, job level Default rate (mean of default ) by employment type, purpose, region Four charts, one sentence each e.g. histogram of Salary , box plot of Salary by Job_Level , scatter of Years_Experience vs Salary e.g. bar chart of the default rate by employment_type , box plot of credit_score by default Three findings with business meaning For the people team For the risk team Tips for the workshop Run the whole audit before you change anything, and keep its output in the notebook: it is the evidence for your decisions. Justify each decision in one line. "We dropped them" is not a justification; "a bill is our target and we cannot know the true value" is. At least one chart must relate a variable to the target : that is the point of the exploration. Run Restart session and run all before you submit. The notebook must run top to bottom. Next session · What drives the monthly bill? The box plot showed that the plan sets the level of the bill, and the scatter plot that data use pushes it up. Next week the commercial team gets a model: a formula that estimates any customer's bill, says how many dollars each gigabyte adds, and is tested on customers it has never seen. Your clean data from this week is where it starts.

Today you build your first model to answer both, and you learn to say honestly how wrong it is. ≈ 85 min 11 ideas Runs in your browser Advance 3 01 Previously at Cordillera Mobile ¶ Last session you cleaned the customer base: duplicates gone, spellings unified, impossible ages and bills fixed. Today the commercial team wants something more useful: a recipe that takes everything we know about a customer and produces an estimate of their bill , and tells us how much each ingredient adds. 02 From a question to a model ¶ Every model starts by naming two things: The target y : what we want to predict. Here, monthly_bill . The features X : what we know about a customer before we see the bill. Plan, contract, data used, minutes, roaming, region, and so on. A model is a recipe that turns features into a prediction. Training the model means letting the data choose the amounts in the recipe. MAE, RMSE, R² ¶ Time to open the envelope. For each test customer, the residual is the actual bill minus the predicted bill. Three numbers summarize the residuals: MAE (mean absolute error): the average miss, in dollars. The easiest to explain. RMSE (root mean squared error): also in dollars, but it squares the misses first, so a few big misses weigh a lot. Too simple (underfitting): it misses real patterns, so it is wrong on the training set and on the test set. Too complex (overfitting): it memorizes the training customers, noise included. Training error looks wonderful; test error is bad. The explainer uses synthetic data (a sine wave with noise) and polynomials of growing degree. Watch the gap between the two errors. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Now on our customers. We compare three recipes, always graded on the same sealed test set: Plan only : the bill is the plan's average. Probably too simple. Full linear model : the 19 features, as above. Every pair of features multiplied ( PolynomialFeatures(degree=2) ): 209 columns, including things like "GB × Unlimited". We train it twice: on a small pilot of 150 customers, and on the whole training set. All pairs, 150 customers (209 columns)" : train_test_mae ( make_pipeline ( PolynomialFeatures ( 2 , include_bias = False ), LinearRegression ()), n = 150 ), "3b. Plan only (3 columns) 3.93 4.17 0.23 2. Full linear model (19 columns) 2.71 2.87 0.16 3a. All pairs, 150 customers (209 columns) 1.08 5.86 4.78 3b. All pairs, 3,489 customers (209 columns) 2.53 2.71 0.17 In [21]: Copied! ax = compare [[ "train MAE" , "test MAE" ]] . plot . barh ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 ), color = [ "tab:blue" , "tab:orange" ]) ax . invert_yaxis () ax . set_title ( "Train vs test error for four recipes" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "MAE (USD)" ) plt . show () ax = compare[["train MAE", "test MAE"]].plot.barh(figsize=(7, 4), color=["tab:blue", "tab:orange"]) ax.invert_yaxis() ax.set_title("Train vs test error for four recipes") ax.set_xlabel("MAE (USD)") plt.show() Read the table from top to bottom: Plan only is wrong by about \$4 everywhere: too simple, it ignores data, roaming and contracts. The full linear model is better on both sets, with a small gap. A healthy model. All pairs on 150 customers is the classic overfit: about \$1 on the customers it trained on, almost \$6 on new ones. 209 columns and only 150 customers is enough to memorize. The same complex recipe on 3,489 customers does not overfit. It even beats the full linear model, because it can learn that Unlimited customers don't pay per GB (remember step 06). The lesson: complexity is not bad in itself. Complexity without enough data is. And the only way to know is to look at the test error, never the training error alone. 09 Cross-validation: one test is one opinion ¶ Our test MAE comes from one particular split. With another random_state , we would get a slightly different number. When we compare models, we don't want to pick a winner because of a lucky split, and we don't want to keep peeking at the sealed test set either. k-fold cross-validation works only inside the training set: it cuts it into k folds, trains on k − 1 and validates on the remaining one, k times. The explainer uses a housing dataset with R² as the score; we do the same with MAE on our customers. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [22]: Copied! scores = cross_val_score ( LinearRegression (), X_train , y_train , cv = 5 , scoring = "neg_mean_absolute_error" ) fold_mae = - scores # scikit-learn reports "bigger is better", so the MAE comes out negative for i , s in enumerate ( fold_mae , start = 1 ): print ( f "Fold { i } : MAE { usd ( s ) } " ) print ( f " \n Cross-validated MAE: { usd ( fold_mae . mean ()) } ± { usd ( fold_mae . std ()) } " ) scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error") fold_mae = -scores # scikit-learn reports "bigger is better", so the MAE comes out negative for i, s in enumerate(fold_mae, start=1): print(f"Fold {i}: MAE {usd(s)}") print(f"\nCross-validated MAE: {usd(fold_mae.mean())} ± {usd(fold_mae.std())}") Fold 1: MAE $2.62 Fold 2: MAE $2.76 Fold 3: MAE $2.80 Fold 4: MAE $2.67 Fold 5: MAE $2.81 Cross-validated MAE: $2.73 ± $0.07 Five opinions instead of one, and they agree: about \$2.73 ± \$0.07 . The spread is small, so the model's quality does not depend on which customers it happened to see. The test MAE (\$2.87) is in the same neighborhood, as it should be. Why the minus sign? scikit-learn always maximizes its scores, so error metrics come out negative ("bigger is better"). We flip the sign to read them in dollars. {"q": "Why do we run <code>cross_val_score</code> on <code>X_train</code> and not on the whole table?", "options": ["Because cross-validation does not work with more than 3,489 rows", "To keep the test set sealed: it is only opened once, for the final grade", "Because the test set has no target column"], "answer": 1, "why": "Cross-validation is for comparing and choosing models. If we used the test set to choose, it would stop being an honest exam. It stays sealed until we report the final result.", "code": false} 10 What we tell the commercial team ¶ Three sentences, with numbers, and no jargon: The plan sets most of the bill: compared with Prepaid, Basic customers pay about \$10 more, Plus \$23 more and Unlimited \$27 more. On top of the plan, international roaming adds about \$8, each GB about \$0.28, and a 24-month contract takes about \$4 off compared with month-to-month. For a new customer we can estimate the bill to within about \$3 (average miss on 1,496 customers the model never saw, on bills that average \$30), which is four times better than guessing the average bill. The price per GB is not the same on every plan (about \$0.53 on Plus, almost nothing on Unlimited); a model that treats plans separately would be more precise, and that is our next step. Notice what's not in the message: no "R²", no "coefficient", no code. The numbers are in dollars, and each sentence answers something the commercial team asked. 11 Your project this week ¶ Today's class is Advance 3 · Ready to model , done on Cordillera.
