Case C follows A or B, depending on whether your target is a number or a category. Everyone adds a short paragraph: what do you expect the model to find, based on your exploratory analysis? Next session · Who is about to leave? The retention team has a different question: not "how much", but " who ". 16.5% of our customers cancel within three months. We'll see why a model that predicts "nobody leaves" is right 83.5% of the time and completely useless, and how to build one that tells the retention team whom to call.
docs.title: What drives the monthly bill?

docs.text: The commercial team at Cordillera Mobile wants two things: to know what actually drives a customer's monthly bill, and to estimate the bill of a customer who has not paid one yet. Today you build your first model to answer both, and you learn to say honestly how wrong it is. ≈ 85 min 11 ideas Runs in your browser Advance 3
docs.title: What drives the monthly bill?

docs.text: Last session you cleaned the customer base: duplicates gone, spellings unified, impossible ages and bills fixed. You ended with 4,985 customers and 15 columns , saved as the clean file we load below. You also saw the first patterns. The clearest one: the bill depends a lot on the plan. Let's load the clean data and look at that again, because today we go from a pattern to a model . In [1]: Copied! import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split , cross_val_score from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error , r2_score CLEAN = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile_clean.csv" df = pd . read_csv ( CLEAN ) print ( f " { df . shape [ 0 ] : , } customers, { df . shape [ 1 ] } columns" ) def usd ( amount ): # format a number as dollars with two decimals, for readable printouts return f "$ { amount : ,.2f } " df . head () import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error, r2_score CLEAN = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile_clean.csv" df = pd.read_csv(CLEAN) print(f"{df.shape[0]:,} customers, {df.shape[1]} columns") def usd(amount): # format a number as dollars with two decimals, for readable printouts return f"${amount:,.2f}" df.head() 4,985 customers, 15 columns Out[1]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id signup_date age region plan contract tenure_months data_gb call_minutes intl_roaming support_tickets autopay payment_method monthly_bill churned 0 CM-12254 2022-07-04 34 Metropolitana Basic 12 months 50 7.1 270 0 2 1 Unknown 25.46 0 1 CM-10173 2026-06-26 31 Centro Plus 12 months 3 19.0 310 0 0 0 Debit card 37.05 1 2 CM-11339 2020-05-29 38 Centro Prepaid Month-to-month 76 3.6 165 0 0 1 Credit card 11.43 0 3 CM-13440 2019-11-02 31 Centro Unlimited 12 months 82 17.8 248 0 2 0 Debit card 40.97 0 4 CM-10214 2022-07-01 34 Metropolitana Basic Month-to-month 50 4.3 240 0 0 0 Cash 19.18 1 In [2]: Copied! avg_bill = df . groupby ( "plan" )[ "monthly_bill" ] . mean () . sort_values () for plan , bill in avg_bill . items (): print ( f " { plan : <10 } average bill { usd ( bill ) : >7 } " ) avg_bill = df.groupby("plan")["monthly_bill"].mean().sort_values() for plan, bill in avg_bill.items(): print(f"{plan: < 10} average bill {usd(bill):>7}") Prepaid average bill $14.79 Basic average bill $24.32 Plus average bill $39.29 Unlimited average bill $46.95 A Prepaid customer pays about \$15 on average and an Unlimited customer about \$47. But the plan is not the whole story: two Plus customers can have very different bills. Data used, minutes, roaming and the contract all seem to play a part. A table of averages answers one question at a time. Today the commercial team wants something more useful: a recipe that takes everything we know about a customer and produces an estimate of their bill , and tells us how much each ingredient adds.
docs.title: 01 Previously at Cordillera Mobile

docs.text: Every model starts by naming two things: The target y : what we want to predict. Here, monthly_bill . The features X : what we know about a customer before we see the bill. Plan, contract, data used, minutes, roaming, region, and so on. A model is a recipe that turns features into a prediction. Training the model means letting the data choose the amounts in the recipe. For a linear regression, the recipe looks like this: bill ≈ starting amount + (amount per GB × GB used) + (amount for roaming × roaming) + … In [3]: Copied! y = df [ "monthly_bill" ] X = df . drop ( columns = [ "customer_id" , "signup_date" , "churned" , "monthly_bill" ]) print ( "Target y:" , y . name , "→" , len ( y ), "values" ) print ( "Features X:" , X . shape [ 1 ], "columns →" , list ( X . columns )) y = df["monthly_bill"] X = df.drop(columns=["customer_id", "signup_date", "churned", "monthly_bill"]) print("Target y:", y.name, "→", len(y), "values") print("Features X:", X.shape[1], "columns →", list(X.columns)) Target y: monthly_bill → 4985 values Features X: 11 columns → ['age', 'region', 'plan', 'contract', 'tenure_months', 'data_gb', 'call_minutes', 'intl_roaming', 'support_tickets', 'autopay', 'payment_method'] We dropped four columns, each for a reason: monthly_bill is the answer. If it stays in X , the model "predicts" the bill by reading it. customer_id is a label, like a name. CM-10001 says nothing about how much someone pays. signup_date is a date, and what it tells us is already in tenure_months . churned is recorded three months after the bill. For a new customer we will never have it. Using information that would not exist at the moment of the prediction is called leakage : the model looks great in class and fails in real life. {"q": "The commercial team wants to estimate the bill of a customer who signs up tomorrow. Which column must not be a feature?", "options": ["data_gb, because it changes every month", "churned, because we only learn it months after the bill", "plan, because it is text"], "answer": 1, "why": "A feature must be known at the moment you make the prediction. Whether a customer cancels is only known three months later, so using it would be leakage. Text columns like plan are fine: we will turn them into numbers in step 04.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 From a question to a model

docs.text: The commercial team will not use the model on the customers we already have: they already know those bills. They will use it on new customers. So the only honest question is: how well does the model do on customers it has never seen? We answer it by setting customers aside before training. The model learns from the training set (70%). The test set (30%) goes into a sealed envelope that we open once, at the very end, to grade the model. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [4]: Copied! X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( X , y , test_size = 0.3 , random_state = 42 ) print ( f "Training set: { len ( X_train ) : , } customers ( { len ( X_train ) / len ( X ) : .0% } )" ) print ( f "Test set: { len ( X_test ) : , } customers ( { len ( X_test ) / len ( X ) : .0% } )" ) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42) print(f"Training set: {len(X_train):,} customers ({len(X_train) / len(X):.0%})") print(f"Test set: {len(X_test):,} customers ({len(X_test) / len(X):.0%})") Training set: 3,489 customers (70%) Test set: 1,496 customers (30%) train_test_split shuffles the rows and cuts them 70/30. random_state=42 fixes the shuffle, so you, your teammates and I get exactly the same split every time we run the notebook. A quick sanity check: the two sets should look alike. If the test set were full of Unlimited customers, it would be a different exam. In [5]: Copied! print ( f "Average bill, training set: { usd ( y_train . mean ()) } " ) print ( f "Average bill, test set: { usd ( y_test . mean ()) } " ) print () print ( pd . DataFrame ({ "train" : X_train [ "plan" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True ), "test" : X_test [ "plan" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True ), }) . round ( 3 )) print(f"Average bill, training set: {usd(y_train.mean())}") print(f"Average bill, test set: {usd(y_test.mean())}") print() print(pd.DataFrame({ "train": X_train["plan"].value_counts(normalize=True), "test": X_test["plan"].value_counts(normalize=True), }).round(3)) Average bill, training set: $30.40 Average bill, test set: $29.78 train test plan Basic 0.305 0.294 Plus 0.289 0.287 Prepaid 0.233 0.253 Unlimited 0.173 0.165 {"q": "A teammate trains the model on all 4,985 customers and reports its error on those same customers. Why is that number not trustworthy?", "options": ["Because 4,985 customers is too few", "Because the model has already seen those bills: it is an exam with the answers", "Because the error should always be computed on the training set"], "answer": 1, "why": "The model was fitted to those exact bills, so its error on them is flattering. A model that memorized them would score perfectly and still fail on tomorrow's customers. Only customers held out before training give an honest grade.", "code": false}
docs.title: 03 Train and test

docs.text: A linear regression multiplies each feature by a number. It can multiply 18 GB by \$0.30, but it cannot multiply "Plus" . Four of our columns are text: plan , contract , region and payment_method . Let's see what happens if we try anyway. In [6]: Copied! try : LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) except Exception as e : print ( type ( e ) . __name__ , "→" , str ( e )[: 120 ]) try: LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) except Exception as e: print(type(e).__name__, "→", str(e)[:120]) ValueError → could not convert string to float: 'Sur' The fix is one-hot encoding : each category gets its own column, with a 1 if the customer belongs to it and 0 otherwise. pandas does it with pd.get_dummies . ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [7]: Copied! sample = X [[ "plan" ]] . head ( 6 ) pd . concat ([ sample , pd . get_dummies ( sample [ "plan" ], prefix = "plan" , dtype = int )], axis = 1 ) sample = X[["plan"]].head(6) pd.concat([sample, pd.get_dummies(sample["plan"], prefix="plan", dtype=int)], axis=1) Out[7]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } plan plan_Basic plan_Plus plan_Prepaid plan_Unlimited 0 Basic 1 0 0 0 1 Plus 0 1 0 0 2 Prepaid 0 0 1 0 3 Unlimited 0 0 0 1 4 Basic 1 0 0 0 5 Plus 0 1 0 0 Every row has exactly one 1, so one column is always redundant: if a customer is not Basic, Plus or Unlimited, they must be Prepaid. drop_first=True removes the first category's column, and that category becomes the reference : the coefficients of the other categories will read as "dollars more (or less) than the reference". pandas drops the first category in alphabetical order unless we say otherwise. That would make Basic the reference plan and "12 months" the reference contract. It reads much better for a manager if the reference is the simplest deal : Prepaid, month-to-month. So we set the order first. In [8]: Copied! X = X . copy () X [ "plan" ] = pd . Categorical ( X [ "plan" ], categories = [ "Prepaid" , "Basic" , "Plus" , "Unlimited" ]) X [ "contract" ] = pd . Categorical ( X [ "contract" ], categories = [ "Month-to-month" , "12 months" , "24 months" ]) X_enc = pd . get_dummies ( X , columns = [ "plan" , "contract" , "region" , "payment_method" ], drop_first = True , dtype = int ) print ( "Before:" , X . shape [ 1 ], "columns After:" , X_enc . shape [ 1 ], "columns" ) print ( list ( X_enc . columns )) X = X.copy() X["plan"] = pd.Categorical(X["plan"], categories=["Prepaid", "Basic", "Plus", "Unlimited"]) X["contract"] = pd.Categorical(X["contract"], categories=["Month-to-month", "12 months", "24 months"]) X_enc = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=["plan", "contract", "region", "payment_method"], drop_first=True, dtype=int) print("Before:", X.shape[1], "columns After:", X_enc.shape[1], "columns") print(list(X_enc.columns)) Before: 11 columns After: 19 columns ['age', 'tenure_months', 'data_gb', 'call_minutes', 'intl_roaming', 'support_tickets', 'autopay', 'plan_Basic', 'plan_Plus', 'plan_Unlimited', 'contract_12 months', 'contract_24 months', 'region_Metropolitana', 'region_Norte', 'region_Sur', 'payment_method_Cash', 'payment_method_Credit card', 'payment_method_Debit card', 'payment_method_Unknown'] 11 columns became 19. docs.title: 04 Categories become numbers

docs.text: Let's start small, with one plan and one feature: for Plus customers, how does the bill grow with the data they use? A straight line through the cloud of points gives an answer: the slope is "dollars per extra GB". But which line? Among all possible lines, linear regression picks the one with the least squares : it makes the sum of the squared vertical misses as small as possible. The explainer below uses a toy example (ad spend and sales) to show what that means. Drag the line and watch the total area of the squares. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [10]: Copied! plus = y_train . index [ X_train [ "plan_Plus" ] == 1 ] # Plus customers in the training set gb_plus = X_train . loc [ plus , [ "data_gb" ]] bill_plus = y_train . loc [ plus ] simple = LinearRegression () . fit ( gb_plus , bill_plus ) print ( f " { len ( plus ) : , } Plus customers in the training set" ) print ( f "Intercept: { usd ( simple . intercept_ ) } Slope: { usd ( simple . coef_ [ 0 ]) } per GB" ) plus = y_train.index[X_train["plan_Plus"] == 1] # Plus customers in the training set gb_plus = X_train.loc[plus, ["data_gb"]] bill_plus = y_train.loc[plus] simple = LinearRegression().fit(gb_plus, bill_plus) print(f"{len(plus):,} Plus customers in the training set") print(f"Intercept: {usd(simple.intercept_)} Slope: {usd(simple.coef_[0])} per GB") 1,008 Plus customers in the training set Intercept: $31.41 Slope: $0.53 per GB In [11]: Copied! grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "data_gb" : np . linspace ( 0 , gb_plus [ "data_gb" ] . max (), 50 )}) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) plt . scatter ( gb_plus [ "data_gb" ], bill_plus , s = 10 , alpha = 0.35 , label = "Plus customers (training set)" ) plt . plot ( grid [ "data_gb" ], simple . predict ( grid ), color = "black" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "least-squares line" ) plt . title ( "Plus plan: the bill grows with data used" ) plt . xlabel ( "Data used last month (GB)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Monthly bill (USD)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () grid = pd.DataFrame({"data_gb": np.linspace(0, gb_plus["data_gb"].max(), 50)}) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.scatter(gb_plus["data_gb"], bill_plus, s=10, alpha=0.35, label="Plus customers (training set)") plt.plot(grid["data_gb"], simple.predict(grid), color="black", linewidth=2.5, label="least-squares line") plt.title("Plus plan: the bill grows with data used") plt.xlabel("Data used last month (GB)") plt.ylabel("Monthly bill (USD)") plt.legend() plt.show() Read it like a manager: a Plus customer pays about \$31 before any data, and each extra GB adds about \$0.53. The cloud around the line is everything else: minutes, roaming, contract, and plain noise. To use everything at once we do multiple regression : the same least-squares idea, but with one coefficient per feature. The code barely changes. In [12]: Copied! model = LinearRegression () model . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( f "Trained on { len ( X_train ) : , } customers and { X_train . shape [ 1 ] } features." ) print ( f "Intercept: { model . intercept_ : .3f } dollars" ) model = LinearRegression() model.fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"Trained on {len(X_train):,} customers and {X_train.shape[1]} features.") print(f"Intercept: {model.intercept_:.3f} dollars") Trained on 3,489 customers and 19 features. Intercept: 10.019 dollars

docs.text: Each coefficient answers one question: if this feature goes up by one, and everything else stays the same, how many dollars does the bill change? For a 0/1 column, "goes up by one" means "belongs to this category instead of the reference". In [13]: Copied! coefs = pd . DataFrame ({ "feature" : X_train . columns , "coefficient" : model . coef_ }) coefs = coefs . sort_values ( "coefficient" , ascending = False ) . round ( 3 ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) coefs coefs = pd.DataFrame({"feature": X_train.columns, "coefficient": model.coef_}) coefs = coefs.sort_values("coefficient", ascending=False).round(3).reset_index(drop=True) coefs Out[13]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } feature coefficient 0 plan_Unlimited 26.701 1 plan_Plus 23.089 2 plan_Basic 10.160 3 intl_roaming 7.951 4 data_gb 0.275 5 payment_method_Unknown 0.244 6 payment_method_Credit card 0.172 7 region_Sur 0.065 8 call_minutes 0.012 9 tenure_months 0.004 10 age 0.000 11 support_tickets -0.033 12 region_Metropolitana -0.052 13 payment_method_Debit card -0.118 14 payment_method_Cash -0.135 15 region_Norte -0.156 16 autopay -0.254 17 contract_12 months -1.861 18 contract_24 months -4.004 Now translate the table into sentences the commercial team can use: Plan, compared with Prepaid: a Basic customer pays about \$10.16 more, Plus \$23.09 more, Unlimited \$26.70 more, with everything else equal. Roaming adds about \$7.95 to the bill. Contract, compared with month-to-month: a 12-month contract is about \$1.86 cheaper, and a 24-month contract about \$4.00 cheaper. Data: each extra GB adds about \$0.28 . Minutes: about \$0.012 each, so 100 extra minutes ≈ \$1.20. Everything else (age, tenure, support tickets, region, payment method, autopay): each moves the bill by about \$0.25 or less. They barely matter. Wait: on Plus the slope was \$0.53 per GB, and now it's \$0.28. The full model has one price per GB for everyone , and Unlimited customers use a lot of data without paying for it. The model splits the difference. Keep that in mind; it comes back in step 08. In [14]: Copied! top = coefs [ coefs [ "coefficient" ] . abs () > 1 ] . sort_values ( "coefficient" ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) plt . barh ( top [ "feature" ], top [ "coefficient" ], color = [ "tab:blue" if c < 0 else "tab:orange" for c in top [ "coefficient" ]]) plt . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 1 ) plt . title ( "The big movers: coefficients larger than 1 dollar" ) plt . xlabel ( "Dollars added to the monthly bill" ) plt . show () top = coefs[coefs["coefficient"].abs() > 1].sort_values("coefficient") plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.barh(top["feature"], top["coefficient"], color=["tab:blue" if c < 0 else "tab:orange" for c in top["coefficient"]]) plt.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=1) plt.title("The big movers: coefficients larger than 1 dollar") plt.xlabel("Dollars added to the monthly bill") plt.show() Careful: a coefficient's size depends on its unit. Minutes has a tiny coefficient (\$0.012), but customers talk hundreds of minutes, so it adds about \$3 to a typical bill. Never rank features by their raw coefficient alone. Now the second request: estimate a new customer's bill . She is 30, lives in the Metropolitana region, just signed a 12-month Plus contract, pays automatically with a credit card, and expects to use 18 GB and 250 minutes a month, without roaming. In [15]: Copied! new_customer = pd . DataFrame ([ dict . fromkeys ( X_train . columns , 0 )]) # one row of zeros with the same columns new_customer . loc [ 0 , [ "age" , "data_gb" , "call_minutes" , "autopay" ]] = [ 30 , 18 , 250 , 1 ] new_customer . loc [ 0 , [ "plan_Plus" , "contract_12 months" , "region_Metropolitana" , "payment_method_Credit card" ]] = 1 estimate = model . predict ( new_customer )[ 0 ] print ( f "Estimated monthly bill: { usd ( estimate ) } " ) new_customer = pd.DataFrame([dict.fromkeys(X_train.columns, 0)]) # one row of zeros with the same columns new_customer.loc[0, ["age", "data_gb", "call_minutes", "autopay"]] = [30, 18, 250, 1] new_customer.loc[0, ["plan_Plus", "contract_12 months", "region_Metropolitana", "payment_method_Credit card"]] = 1 estimate = model.predict(new_customer)[0] print(f"Estimated monthly bill: {usd(estimate)}") Estimated monthly bill: $39.06 Where does that number come from? docs.title: 06 Reading the coefficients like a manager

docs.text: Time to open the envelope. For each test customer, the residual is the actual bill minus the predicted bill. Three numbers summarize the residuals: MAE (mean absolute error): the average miss, in dollars. The easiest to explain. RMSE (root mean squared error): also in dollars, but it squares the misses first, so a few big misses weigh a lot. R² : the share of the differences between customers' bills that the model explains. 1 is perfect; 0 is no better than predicting the average bill for everyone. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [16]: Copied! def report ( name , y_true , y_pred ): return { "set" : name , "MAE" : mean_absolute_error ( y_true , y_pred ), "RMSE" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_true , y_pred )), "R2" : r2_score ( y_true , y_pred ), } pred_train = model . predict ( X_train ) pred_test = model . predict ( X_test ) metrics = pd . DataFrame ([ report ( "train" , y_train , pred_train ), report ( "test" , y_test , pred_test )]) . set_index ( "set" ) metrics . round ( 3 ) def report(name, y_true, y_pred): return { "set": name, "MAE": mean_absolute_error(y_true, y_pred), "RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_true, y_pred)), "R2": r2_score(y_true, y_pred), } pred_train = model.predict(X_train) pred_test = model.predict(X_test) metrics = pd.DataFrame([report("train", y_train, pred_train), report("test", y_test, pred_test)]).set_index("set") metrics.round(3) Out[16]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE R2 set train 2.706 3.433 0.928 test 2.870 3.560 0.924 In [17]: Copied! mae = mean_absolute_error ( y_test , pred_test ) print ( f "On customers it has never seen, the model misses by { usd ( mae ) } on average," ) print ( f "on bills that average { usd ( y_test . mean ()) } . It explains { r2_score ( y_test , pred_test ) : .0% } of the differences between bills." ) mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred_test) print(f"On customers it has never seen, the model misses by {usd(mae)} on average,") print(f"on bills that average {usd(y_test.mean())}. It explains {r2_score(y_test, pred_test):.0%} of the differences between bills.") On customers it has never seen, the model misses by $2.87 on average, on bills that average $29.78. It explains 92% of the differences between bills. Is \$2.87 good? A number means little without a comparison. The simplest possible "model" predicts the same bill for everyone: the average of the training set. That is our baseline . In [18]: Copied! baseline = np . full ( len ( y_test ), y_train . mean ()) print ( f "Baseline (always predict { usd ( y_train . mean ()) } ): MAE { usd ( mean_absolute_error ( y_test , baseline )) } " ) print ( f "Our linear regression: MAE { usd ( mae ) } " ) baseline = np.full(len(y_test), y_train.mean()) print(f"Baseline (always predict {usd(y_train.mean())}): MAE {usd(mean_absolute_error(y_test, baseline))}") print(f"Our linear regression: MAE {usd(mae)}") Baseline (always predict $30.40): MAE $11.27 Our linear regression: MAE $2.87 In [19]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) plt . scatter ( pred_test , y_test , s = 10 , alpha = 0.35 ) lims = [ 0 , y_test . max () + 5 ] plt . plot ( lims , lims , color = "black" , linewidth = 1.5 , label = "perfect prediction" ) plt . title ( "Test set: actual vs predicted bill" ) plt . xlabel ( "Predicted bill (USD)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Actual bill (USD)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.scatter(pred_test, y_test, s=10, alpha=0.35) lims = [0, y_test.max() + 5] plt.plot(lims, lims, color="black", linewidth=1.5, label="perfect prediction") plt.title("Test set: actual vs predicted bill") plt.xlabel("Predicted bill (USD)") plt.ylabel("Actual bill (USD)") plt.legend() plt.show() The points hug the diagonal: the model is about four times more accurate than the baseline. Train and test errors are close (\$2.71 vs \$2.87), which is the sign we want: the model learned patterns that also hold for new customers, instead of memorizing. RMSE (\$3.56) is a bit above MAE, which tells us there are no huge misses: when a few customers are off by a lot, RMSE pulls far away from MAE. {"q": "Two models have the same MAE: 3 dollars. Model A has an RMSE of 3.4 dollars; model B, 7.9 dollars. What does that tell you?", "options": ["Model B is better, because a higher RMSE means more explained variation", "Model B has a few very large misses; model A's misses are more even", "Nothing: RMSE and MAE always move together"], "answer": 1, "why": "RMSE squares each miss before averaging, so a handful of big misses inflate it much more than MAE. If a surprise bill 20 dollars too high is what makes customers call to cancel, model A is the safer choice.", "code": false}
docs.title: 07 How wrong are we? MAE, RMSE, R²

docs.text: A model can fail in two opposite ways. Too simple (underfitting): it misses real patterns, so it is wrong on the training set and on the test set. Too complex (overfitting): it memorizes the training customers, noise included. Training error looks wonderful; test error is bad. The explainer uses synthetic data (a sine wave with noise) and polynomials of growing degree. Watch the gap between the two errors. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Now on our customers. We compare three recipes, always graded on the same sealed test set: Plan only : the bill is the plan's average. Probably too simple. Full linear model : the 19 features, as above. Every pair of features multiplied ( PolynomialFeatures(degree=2) ): 209 columns, including things like "GB × Unlimited". We train it twice: on a small pilot of 150 customers, and on the whole training set. In [20]: Copied! from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline def train_test_mae ( estimator , cols = None , n = None ): Xa = X_train if cols is None else X_train [ cols ] Xb = X_test if cols is None else X_test [ cols ] Xa , ya = ( Xa , y_train ) if n is None else ( Xa . iloc [: n ], y_train . iloc [: n ]) estimator . fit ( Xa , ya ) return mean_absolute_error ( ya , estimator . predict ( Xa )), mean_absolute_error ( y_test , estimator . predict ( Xb )) plan_cols = [ "plan_Basic" , "plan_Plus" , "plan_Unlimited" ] rows = { "1. Plan only (3 columns)" : train_test_mae ( LinearRegression (), cols = plan_cols ), "2. Full linear model (19 columns)" : train_test_mae ( LinearRegression ()), "3a. All pairs, 150 customers (209 columns)" : train_test_mae ( make_pipeline ( PolynomialFeatures ( 2 , include_bias = False ), LinearRegression ()), n = 150 ), "3b. All pairs, 3,489 customers (209 columns)" : train_test_mae ( make_pipeline ( PolynomialFeatures ( 2 , include_bias = False ), LinearRegression ())), } compare = pd . DataFrame ( rows , index = [ "train MAE" , "test MAE" ]) . T compare [ "gap" ] = compare [ "test MAE" ] - compare [ "train MAE" ] compare . round ( 2 ) from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline def train_test_mae(estimator, cols=None, n=None): Xa = X_train if cols is None else X_train[cols] Xb = X_test if cols is None else X_test[cols] Xa, ya = (Xa, y_train) if n is None else (Xa.iloc[:n], y_train.iloc[:n]) estimator.fit(Xa, ya) return mean_absolute_error(ya, estimator.predict(Xa)), mean_absolute_error(y_test, estimator.predict(Xb)) plan_cols = ["plan_Basic", "plan_Plus", "plan_Unlimited"] rows = { "1. Plan only (3 columns)": train_test_mae(LinearRegression(), cols=plan_cols), "2. Full linear model (19 columns)": train_test_mae(LinearRegression()), "3a. All pairs, 150 customers (209 columns)": train_test_mae(make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2, include_bias=False), LinearRegression()), n=150), "3b. All pairs, 3,489 customers (209 columns)": train_test_mae(make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(2, include_bias=False), LinearRegression())), } compare = pd.DataFrame(rows, index=["train MAE", "test MAE"]).T compare["gap"] = compare["test MAE"] - compare["train MAE"] compare.round(2) Out[20]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } train MAE test MAE gap 1. Plan only (3 columns) 3.93 4.17 0.23 2. Full linear model (19 columns) 2.71 2.87 0.16 3a. All pairs, 150 customers (209 columns) 1.08 5.86 4.78 3b. All pairs, 3,489 customers (209 columns) 2.53 2.71 0.17 In [21]: Copied! ax = compare [[ "train MAE" , "test MAE" ]] . plot . barh ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 ), color = [ "tab:blue" , "tab:orange" ]) ax . invert_yaxis () ax . set_title ( "Train vs test error for four recipes" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "MAE (USD)" ) plt . show () ax = compare[["train MAE", "test MAE"]].plot.barh(figsize=(7, 4), color=["tab:blue", "tab:orange"]) ax.invert_yaxis() ax.set_title("Train vs test error for four recipes") ax.set_xlabel("MAE (USD)") plt.show() Read the table from top to bottom: Plan only is wrong by about \$4 everywhere: too simple, it ignores data, roaming and contracts. The full linear model is better on both sets, with a small gap. A healthy model. All pairs on 150 customers is the classic overfit: about \$1 on the customers it trained on, almost \$6 on new ones. 209 columns and only 150 customers is enough to memorize. The same complex recipe on 3,489 customers does not overfit. It even beats the full linear model, because it can learn that Unlimited customers don't pay per GB (remember step 06). The lesson: complexity is not bad in itself. Complexity without enough data is. And the only way to know is to look at the test error, never the training error alone.
docs.title: 08 Too simple, too complex

docs.text: Our test MAE comes from one particular split. With another random_state , we would get a slightly different number. When we compare models, we don't want to pick a winner because of a lucky split, and we don't want to keep peeking at the sealed test set either. k-fold cross-validation works only inside the training set: it cuts it into k folds, trains on k − 1 and validates on the remaining one, k times. The explainer uses a housing dataset with R² as the score; we do the same with MAE on our customers. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [22]: Copied! scores = cross_val_score ( LinearRegression (), X_train , y_train , cv = 5 , scoring = "neg_mean_absolute_error" ) fold_mae = - scores # scikit-learn reports "bigger is better", so the MAE comes out negative for i , s in enumerate ( fold_mae , start = 1 ): print ( f "Fold { i } : MAE { usd ( s ) } " ) print ( f " \n Cross-validated MAE: { usd ( fold_mae . mean ()) } ± { usd ( fold_mae . std ()) } " ) scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error") fold_mae = -scores # scikit-learn reports "bigger is better", so the MAE comes out negative for i, s in enumerate(fold_mae, start=1): print(f"Fold {i}: MAE {usd(s)}") print(f"\nCross-validated MAE: {usd(fold_mae.mean())} ± {usd(fold_mae.std())}") Fold 1: MAE $2.62 Fold 2: MAE $2.76 Fold 3: MAE $2.80 Fold 4: MAE $2.67 Fold 5: MAE $2.81 Cross-validated MAE: $2.73 ± $0.07 Five opinions instead of one, and they agree: about \$2.73 ± \$0.07 . The spread is small, so the model's quality does not depend on which customers it happened to see. The test MAE (\$2.87) is in the same neighborhood, as it should be. Why the minus sign? scikit-learn always maximizes its scores, so error metrics come out negative ("bigger is better"). We flip the sign to read them in dollars. {"q": "Why do we run cross_val_score on X_train and not on the whole table?", "options": ["Because cross-validation does not work with more than 3,489 rows", "To keep the test set sealed: it is only opened once, for the final grade", "Because the test set has no target column"], "answer": 1, "why": "Cross-validation is for comparing and choosing models. If we used the test set to choose, it would stop being an honest exam. It stays sealed until we report the final result.", "code": false}
docs.title: 09 Cross-validation: one test is one opinion

docs.text: Three sentences, with numbers, and no jargon: The plan sets most of the bill: compared with Prepaid, Basic customers pay about \$10 more, Plus \$23 more and Unlimited \$27 more. On top of the plan, international roaming adds about \$8, each GB about \$0.28, and a 24-month contract takes about \$4 off compared with month-to-month. For a new customer we can estimate the bill to within about \$3 (average miss on 1,496 customers the model never saw, on bills that average \$30), which is four times better than guessing the average bill. The price per GB is not the same on every plan (about \$0.53 on Plus, almost nothing on Unlimited); a model that treats plans separately would be more precise, and that is our next step. Notice what's not in the message: no "R²", no "coefficient", no code. The numbers are in dollars, and each sentence answers something the commercial team asked.

By the end of this class you will have a model that gives every customer a probability of leaving, and a calling list chosen with money, not habit. ≈ 85 min 8 ideas Runs in your browser Advance 4 01 Previously at Cordillera Mobile ¶ Last session the commercial team asked what drives a customer's monthly bill. A linear regression answered it: the plan, the data used and roaming explain about 92% of the variation in bills, and the model is off by about USD 3 on average. Today the retention team knocks on the door. Their question is different: will this customer cancel in the next three months? The answer is not a number of dollars but yes or no . That is a classification problem, and it needs a new model and, above all, new ways to judge it. We start from the clean customer base we built in session 2. If churn is rare, a model can look brilliant while being useless. The usual score, accuracy , is the share of customers the model classifies correctly. It sounds like exactly what we want. Let's see. With a rare class, always stratify. 04 From a line to a probability ¶ Why not reuse last week's linear regression, with churned (0 or 1) as the target? Its prediction would be a number we could read as "chance of leaving". Let's try it and look at the predictions. In [9]: Copied! from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression line = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) pred_line = line . predict ( X_test ) print ( f "Lowest prediction: { pred_line . min () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Highest prediction: { pred_line . max () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Customers with a 'probability' below 0: { ( pred_line < 0 ) . sum () } " ) from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression line = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) pred_line = line.predict(X_test) print(f"Lowest prediction: {pred_line.min():.2f}") print(f"Highest prediction: {pred_line.max():.2f}") print(f"Customers with a 'probability' below 0: {(pred_line < 0).sum()}") Lowest prediction: -0.18 Highest prediction: 0.62 Customers with a 'probability' below 0: 133 A probability of −0.18 means nothing. A straight line keeps going forever, so with enough tickets or enough tenure it leaves the range from 0 to 1. Logistic regression fixes this in two steps. First it computes a score exactly like a linear regression: $z = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots$ Then it squeezes that score through the sigmoid curve, $p = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, which bends every number into the range 0 to 1. Large positive scores become probabilities near 1, large negative ones near 0, and a score of 0 becomes exactly 0.5. In the explainer, switch between the two models and move the weight and the intercept to reshape the S. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [10]: Copied! def sigmoid ( z ): return 1 / ( 1 + np . exp ( - z )) for z in [ - 4 , - 2 , 0 , 2 , 4 ]: print ( f "score z = { z : +d } → probability { sigmoid ( z ) : .2f } " ) def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) for z in [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4]: print(f"score z = {z:+d} → probability {sigmoid(z):.2f}") score z = -4 → probability 0.02 score z = -2 → probability 0.12 score z = +0 → probability 0.50 score z = +2 → probability 0.88 score z = +4 → probability 0.98 In [11]: Copied! z = np . linspace ( - 6 , 6 , 200 ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 3.5 )) plt . plot ( z , sigmoid ( z ), lw = 2.5 , label = "logistic: always between 0 and 1" ) plt . plot ( z , 0.5 + z / 8 , ls = "--" , label = "a straight line: leaves [0, 1]" ) plt . axhline ( 0 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . axhline ( 1 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . ylim ( - 0.4 , 1.4 ) plt . title ( "The sigmoid squeezes any score into a probability" ) plt . xlabel ( "score z" ) plt . ylabel ( "predicted value" ) plt . legend () plt . show () z = np.linspace(-6, 6, 200) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5)) plt.plot(z, sigmoid(z), lw=2.5, label="logistic: always between 0 and 1") plt.plot(z, 0.5 + z / 8, ls="--", label="a straight line: leaves [0, 1]") plt.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.axhline(1, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.ylim(-0.4, 1.4) plt.title("The sigmoid squeezes any score into a probability") plt.xlabel("score z") plt.ylabel("predicted value") plt.legend() plt.show() 05 Training the logistic regression ¶ In scikit-learn the model is LogisticRegression . We put a StandardScaler in front of it, inside a Pipeline . The scaler puts every feature on the same scale (mean 0, standard deviation 1), for two reasons: the solver that fits the model converges faster and more reliably when tenure (months) and call minutes (hundreds) are not on wildly different scales; later, the coefficients become comparable: each one says how much one standard deviation of that feature moves the score. The pipeline learns the scaling from the training set only, then applies it to any data you give it. In [12]: Copied! from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression model = Pipeline ([ ( "scale" , StandardScaler ()), ( "logit" , LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 2000 )), ]) model . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( "Trained on" , len ( X_train ), "customers" ) from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression model = Pipeline([ ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("logit", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)), ]) model.fit(X_train, y_train) print("Trained on", len(X_train), "customers") Trained on 3738 customers predict_proba returns two columns per customer: the probability of class 0 (stays) and of class 1 (leaves). We keep the second one. Here are six test customers with their probability of leaving. In [13]: Copied! p_test = model . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ] show = df . loc [ X_test . index , [ "customer_id" , "contract" , "tenure_months" , "support_tickets" , "region" , "churned" ]] . copy () show [ "p_churn" ] = p_test . round ( 2 ) show . sample ( 6 , random_state = 42 ) . sort_values ( "p_churn" , ascending = False ) p_test = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] show = df.loc[X_test.index, ["customer_id", "contract", "tenure_months", "support_tickets", "region", "churned"]].copy() show["p_churn"] = p_test.round(2) show.sample(6, random_state=42).sort_values("p_churn", ascending=False) Out[13]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id contract tenure_months support_tickets region churned p_churn 1372 CM-10824 Month-to-month 1 1 Sur 0 0.56 2473 CM-12797 Month-to-month 13 3 Metropolitana 1 0.47 4126 CM-11834 Month-to-month 43 1 Centro 1 0.12 4073 CM-14545 Month-to-month 76 0 Sur 0 0.08 956 CM-11709 24 months 14 0 Metropolitana 0 0.05 3353 CM-14086 12 months 56 0 Metropolitana 0 0.03 In [14]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) sns . histplot ( x = p_test , hue = y_test . map ({ 0 : "stayed" , 1 : "left" }), hue_order = [ "stayed" , "left" ], palette = { "stayed" : "tab:blue" , "left" : "tab:orange" }, bins = 30 , stat = "density" , common_norm = False , element = "step" ) plt . title ( "Predicted probability of leaving, test customers" ) plt . xlabel ( "predicted probability of churn" ) plt . ylabel ( "density" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) sns.histplot(x=p_test, hue=y_test.map({0: "stayed", 1: "left"}), hue_order=["stayed", "left"], palette={"stayed": "tab:blue", "left": "tab:orange"}, bins=30, stat="density", common_norm=False, element="step") plt.title("Predicted probability of leaving, test customers") plt.xlabel("predicted probability of churn") plt.ylabel("density") plt.show() The customers who really left (orange) tend to get higher probabilities, but the two groups overlap a lot. No single cut-off will separate them perfectly. That overlap is why the next two sections exist. 06 The confusion matrix ¶ To turn probabilities into a decision we need a threshold : call the customer if $p \geq$ threshold. The default of model.predict() is 0.5. Each test customer then lands in one of four cells: True positive (TP): we call, and they were leaving. Money well spent. False positive (FP): we call, but they would have stayed. A wasted offer. False negative (FN): we don't call, and they leave. A lost customer. True negative (TN): we don't call, and they stay. Nothing happens. In [15]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix pred_05 = model . predict ( X_test ) # threshold 0.5 tn , fp , fn , tp = confusion_matrix ( y_test , pred_05 ) . ravel () print ( f "True positives (called, were leaving): { tp } " ) print ( f "False positives (called, would stay): { fp } " ) print ( f "False negatives (not called, left): { fn } " ) print ( f "True negatives (not called, stayed): { tn } " ) from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix pred_05 = model.predict(X_test) # threshold 0.5 tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred_05).ravel() print(f"True positives (called, were leaving): {tp}") print(f"False positives (called, would stay): {fp}") print(f"False negatives (not called, left): {fn}") print(f"True negatives (not called, stayed): {tn}") True positives (called, were leaving): 30 False positives (called, would stay): 10 False negatives (not called, left): 175 True negatives (not called, stayed): 1032 In [16]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 4.5 , 4 )) ConfusionMatrixDisplay . from_predictions ( y_test , pred_05 , display_labels = [ "stays" , "leaves" ], cmap = "Oranges" , colorbar = False , ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Threshold 0.5, test customers" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "predicted" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "actual" ) plt . show () from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4)) ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions( y_test, pred_05, display_labels=["stays", "leaves"], cmap="Oranges", colorbar=False, ax=ax ) ax.set_title("Threshold 0.5, test customers") ax.set_xlabel("predicted") ax.set_ylabel("actual") plt.show() Each metric reads the matrix from a different angle: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the customers we call, how many were really leaving? How well do we spend the offers? Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the customers who leave, how many do we call? How many leavers do we reach? F1 : a single number that balances the two (their harmonic mean). AUC : forget the threshold. Pick a random leaver and a random stayer: how often does the model give the leaver the higher probability? 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. Session 5 draws the curve behind it. In [17]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import precision_score , f1_score , roc_auc_score print ( f "Accuracy: { accuracy_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .1% } (the lazy model: { 1 - y_test . mean () : .1% } )" ) print ( f "Precision: { precision_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } " ) print ( f "Recall: { recall_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } " ) print ( f "F1: { f1_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } " ) print ( f "AUC: { roc_auc_score ( y_test , p_test ) : .2f } " ) from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, f1_score, roc_auc_score print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, pred_05):.1%} (the lazy model: {1 - y_test.mean():.1%})") print(f"Precision: {precision_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f}") print(f"Recall: {recall_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f}") print(f"F1: {f1_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f}") print(f"AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test):.2f}") Accuracy: 85.2% (the lazy model: 83.6%) Precision: 0.75 Recall: 0.15 F1: 0.24 AUC: 0.72 In [18]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import classification_report print ( classification_report ( y_test , pred_05 , target_names = [ "stays" , "leaves" ])) from sklearn.metrics import classification_report print(classification_report(y_test, pred_05, target_names=["stays", "leaves"])) precision recall f1-score support stays 0.86 0.99 0.92 1042 leaves 0.75 0.15 0.24 205 accuracy 0.85 1247 macro avg 0.80 0.57 0.58 1247 weighted avg 0.84 0.85 0.81 1247 Read it like the retention manager would. When we call someone, we are right 3 times out of 4 (precision 0.75). But we only call 40 customers and reach 30 of the 205 leavers (recall 0.15). Accuracy (85.2%) barely beats the lazy model, yet the AUC of 0.72 says the ranking carries real signal. The problem is not the model; it is the threshold. The explainer below uses a toy example (customers buying a travel package), but the mechanism is identical: moving the threshold never changes the model, it moves customers between the cells of the matrix. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [19]: Copied! for t in [ 0.5 , 0.3 , 0.2 ]: pred_t = ( p_test >= t ) . astype ( int ) print ( f "threshold { t : .1f } : calls { pred_t . sum () : 4d } " f "precision { precision_score ( y_test , pred_t ) : .2f } recall { recall_score ( y_test , pred_t ) : .2f } " ) for t in [0.5, 0.3, 0.2]: pred_t = (p_test >= t).astype(int) print(f"threshold {t:.1f}: calls {pred_t.sum():4d} " f"precision {precision_score(y_test, pred_t):.2f} recall {recall_score(y_test, pred_t):.2f}") threshold 0.5: calls 40 precision 0.75 recall 0.15 threshold 0.3: calls 180 precision 0.39 recall 0.34 threshold 0.2: calls 341 precision 0.33 recall 0.55 {"q": "The retention team lowers the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2. What happens?", "options": ["Recall goes up and precision goes down: more leavers reached, more offers wasted", "Both precision and recall go up, because the model gets better", "Nothing changes: the threshold is part of the trained model"], "answer": 0, "why": "A lower bar means more customers get called. More of the leavers are among them (recall up), but so are more stayers (precision down). The model itself is untouched.", "code": false} 07 Choosing the threshold with money, not habit ¶ 0.5 is a habit, not a decision. The right threshold depends on what each mistake costs Cordillera. Finance gives us two numbers: a missed churner (false negative) costs about USD 300 in lost margin; every offer costs about USD 40 , whether the customer was leaving or not. On a stayer it is simply wasted. We assume the offer keeps the leavers we call (optimistic, but a fine start). Then the total cost of a calling list is $$\text{cost} = 40 \times \text{customers called} + 300 \times \text{churners not called}.$$ In the explainer, the curve is that cost for every threshold, computed on our 1,247 test customers. Change the two costs and watch the cheapest threshold move. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [20]: Copied! COST_MISS = 300 # USD lost when a churner leaves without a call COST_OFFER = 40 # USD per call with an offer def total_cost ( threshold ): called = p_test >= threshold missed = ( ~ called ) & ( y_test . values == 1 ) return COST_OFFER * called . sum () + COST_MISS * missed . sum () print ( f "Call nobody: USD { COST_MISS * y_test . sum () : , } " ) print ( f "Call everyone: USD { COST_OFFER * len ( y_test ) : , } " ) print ( f "Threshold 0.5: USD { total_cost ( 0.5 ) : , } " ) COST_MISS = 300 # USD lost when a churner leaves without a call COST_OFFER = 40 # USD per call with an offer def total_cost(threshold): called = p_test >= threshold missed = (~called) & (y_test.values == 1) return COST_OFFER * called.sum() + COST_MISS * missed.sum() print(f"Call nobody: USD {COST_MISS * y_test.sum():,}") print(f"Call everyone: USD {COST_OFFER * len(y_test):,}") print(f"Threshold 0.5: USD {total_cost(0.5):,}") Call nobody: USD 61,500 Call everyone: USD 49,880 Threshold 0.5: USD 54,100 In [21]: Copied! thresholds = np . round ( np . arange ( 0.05 , 0.951 , 0.01 ), 2 ) costs = pd . best = costs . loc [ costs [ "cost_usd" ] . idxmin ()] print ( f "Cheapest threshold: { best [ 'threshold' ] : .2f } " ) print ( f " calls { int ( best [ 'calls' ]) } customers, total cost USD { int ( best [ 'cost_usd' ]) : , } " ) print ( f " versus threshold 0.5: USD { total_cost ( 0.5 ) - best [ 'cost_usd' ] : ,.0f } cheaper" ) best = costs.loc[costs["cost_usd"].idxmin()] print(f"Cheapest threshold: {best['threshold']:.2f}") print(f" calls {int(best['calls'])} customers, total cost USD {int(best['cost_usd']):,}") print(f" versus threshold 0.5: USD {total_cost(0.5) - best['cost_usd']:,.0f} cheaper") Cheapest threshold: 0.13 calls 575 customers, total cost USD 39,800 versus threshold 0.5: USD 14,300 cheaper In [23]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) plt . plot ( costs [ "threshold" ], costs [ "cost_usd" ] / 1000 , lw = 2.5 ) plt . scatter ([ best [ "threshold" ]], [ best [ "cost_usd" ] / 1000 ], s = 60 , zorder = 3 , label = f "cheapest: { best [ 'threshold' ] : .2f } " ) plt . scatter ([ 0.5 ], [ total_cost ( 0.5 ) / 1000 ], s = 60 , zorder = 3 , label = "the habit: 0.50" ) plt . title ( "Total cost of the calling list, test customers" ) plt . xlabel ( "threshold" ) plt . ylabel ( "total cost (thousand USD)" ) plt . legend () plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) plt.plot(costs["threshold"], costs["cost_usd"] / 1000, lw=2.5) plt.scatter([best["threshold"]], [best["cost_usd"] / 1000], s=60, zorder=3, label=f"cheapest: {best['threshold']:.2f}") plt.scatter([0.5], [total_cost(0.5) / 1000], s=60, zorder=3, label="the habit: 0.50") plt.title("Total cost of the calling list, test customers") plt.xlabel("threshold") plt.ylabel("total cost (thousand USD)") plt.legend() plt.show() The cheapest threshold is 0.13 : call 575 customers for a total of USD 39,800, against USD 54,100 at 0.5. And 0.13 is no coincidence. Calling a customer with probability $p$ costs 40; not calling costs, on average, $300 \times p$. Calling pays off as soon as $300p > 40$, that is $p > 40/300 \approx 0.13$. The break-even threshold is the ratio of the two costs. One honest caveat: we picked the threshold on the test set. In a real project you would choose it on a validation set (or with cross-validation) and keep the test set for the final, untouched check. {"q": "Finance revises the numbers: the offer now costs USD 100 instead of 40, and a lost churner still costs 300. Where does the best threshold move?", "options": ["Down, to call more customers", "Up, to about 0.33: each call must be more certain to be worth it", "It stays at 0.13, because the model has not changed"], "answer": 1, "why": "Calling pays off when 300 × p is larger than the offer cost, so the break-even moves to 100 / 300 ≈ 0.33 (in the explainer, the cheapest list on our test customers lands at 0.39, close to it). Dearer offers mean a shorter, surer calling list.", "code": false} 08 What drives churn ¶ The retention team will ask why . Because we scaled the features, the coefficients are comparable: each one says how much a one-standard-deviation change in that feature pushes the score (and so the probability) of leaving. Positive pushes towards leaving, negative towards staying. The dummies compare against the baseline: a Prepaid customer on a month-to-month contract in the Centro region, paying by bank transfer. In [24]: Copied! coefs = pd . Series ( model . named_steps [ "logit" ] . coef_ [ 0 ], index = X . columns ) . sort_values () print ( coefs . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) coefs = pd.Series(model.named_steps["logit"].coef_[0], index=X.columns).sort_values() print(coefs.round(2).to_string()) contract_12 months -0.60 contract_24 months -0.51 plan_Unlimited -0.48 tenure_months -0.35 autopay -0.31 plan_Plus -0.07 age -0.05 plan_Basic -0.04 payment_method_Cash -0.03 call_minutes 0.01 payment_method_Unknown 0.02 intl_roaming 0.06 payment_method_Debit card 0.08 payment_method_Credit card 0.08 data_gb 0.09 region_Sur 0.12 region_Metropolitana 0.19 region_Norte 0.37 support_tickets 0.40 monthly_bill 0.40 In [25]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 5.5 )) colors = [ "tab:blue" if c < 0 else "tab:orange" for c in coefs ] plt . barh ( coefs . index , coefs . values , color = colors ) plt . axvline ( 0 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . title ( "Logistic regression coefficients (scaled features)" ) plt . xlabel ( "← pushes towards staying pushes towards leaving →" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5.5)) colors = ["tab:blue" if c < 0 else "tab:orange" for c in coefs] plt.barh(coefs.index, coefs.values, color=colors) plt.axvline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.title("Logistic regression coefficients (scaled features)") plt.xlabel("← pushes towards staying pushes towards leaving →") plt.show() Reading it carefully: Contracts protect. A 12- or 24-month contract has the strongest negative coefficients: those customers leave much less than month-to-month ones. Complaints and bills push out. More support_tickets and a higher monthly_bill raise the risk, and so does living in the Norte region. Loyalty and autopay protect. Longer tenure_months , autopay and an Unlimited plan go with staying. Age, call minutes and payment method barely matter. These are associations, not causes . The model says customers on contracts leave less; it does not prove that signing someone onto a contract will keep them. Still, it tells the team where to look. In [26]: Copied! # Checking two stories against the raw churn rates print ( df . groupby ( "contract" )[ "churned" ] . mean () . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) . to_string ()) print () norte = df [ "region" ] == "Norte" many_tickets = df [ "support_tickets" ] >= 2 print ( f "Norte, 2+ tickets: { df . loc [ norte & many_tickets , 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "Everyone else: { df . loc [ ~ ( norte & many_tickets ), 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "New customers (< 6 months): { df . loc [ df [ 'tenure_months' ] < 6 , 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) # Checking two stories against the raw churn rates print(df.groupby("contract")["churned"].mean().map("{:.1%}".format).to_string()) print() norte = df["region"] == "Norte" many_tickets = df["support_tickets"] >= 2 print(f"Norte, 2+ tickets: {df.loc[norte & many_tickets, 'churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"Everyone else: {df.loc[~(norte & many_tickets), 'churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"New customers ( < 6 months): {df.loc[df['tenure_months'] < 6, 'churned'].mean():.1%}") contract 12 months 8.9% 24 months 7.8% Month-to-month 22.0% Norte, 2+ tickets: 51.1% Everyone else: 14.1% New customers (< 6 months): 44.4% The raw rates back it up, and they suggest three concrete actions: Offer contracts to month-to-month customers, the group with the highest churn. Fix support in the north : Norte customers with two or more complaints leave far more than anyone else. That is a coverage and service problem, not a pricing one. Look after new customers : in their first six months they leave at a much higher rate, so onboarding matters. Notice that some of these patterns are thresholds ("2 or more tickets", "under 6 months") that a single straight score handles only roughly. Keep that in mind for session 5. {"q": "The coefficient of <code>autopay</code> is negative. Which statement can you defend in front of the retention team?", "options": ["Turning on autopay for a customer will make them stay", "Customers with autopay tend to leave less, other things equal; it is worth testing whether promoting autopay helps", "Autopay is the most important reason customers stay"], "answer": 1, "why": "A coefficient shows an association in historical data, not a cause. And with contracts and Unlimited further from zero, autopay is not the strongest factor either. The honest move is to test it.", "code": false} 09 What we tell the retention team ¶ Let's put the options side by side, on the 1,247 test customers the model never saw. In [27]: Copied! def strategy ( name , called ): called = np . asarray ( called , dtype = bool ) reached = ( called & ( y_test . values == 1 )) . sum () cost = COST_OFFER * called . sum () + COST_MISS * ( y_test . sum () - reached ) return { "strategy" : name , "calls" : called . sum (), "churners reached" : reached , "cost_usd" : cost } t_best = best [ "threshold" ] plan = pd . DataFrame ([ strategy ( "Call nobody" , np . zeros ( len ( y_test ))), strategy ( "Call everyone" , np . ones ( len ( y_test ))), strategy ( "Model, threshold 0.50" , p_test >= 0.5 ), strategy ( f "Model, threshold { t_best : .2f } " , p_test >= t_best ), ]) plan [ "saved vs nobody" ] = plan [ "cost_usd" ] . iloc [ 0 ] - plan [ "cost_usd" ] plan def strategy(name, called): called = np.asarray(called, dtype=bool) reached = (called & (y_test.values == 1)).sum() cost = COST_OFFER * called.sum() + COST_MISS * (y_test.sum() - reached) return {"strategy": name, "calls": called.sum(), "churners reached": reached, "cost_usd": cost} t_best = best["threshold"] plan = pd.DataFrame([ strategy("Call nobody", np.zeros(len(y_test))), strategy("Call everyone", np.ones(len(y_test))), strategy("Model, threshold 0.50", p_test >= 0.5), strategy(f"Model, threshold {t_best:.2f}", p_test >= t_best), ]) plan["saved vs nobody"] = plan["cost_usd"].iloc[0] - plan["cost_usd"] plan Out[27]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } strategy calls churners reached cost_usd saved vs nobody 0 Call nobody 0 0 61500 0 1 Call everyone 1247 205 49880 11620 2 Model, threshold 0.50 40 30 54100 7400 3 Model, threshold 0.13 575 149 39800 21700 Calling nobody costs USD 61,500 in lost customers. Calling everyone costs USD 49,880. The model at 0.5 is cheaper than nobody but worse than everyone, because it calls too few. The model at 0.13 calls 575 customers (46% of the base), reaches 149 of the 205 leavers and costs USD 39,800: USD 21,700 less than doing nothing and about USD 10,000 less than calling everyone. The message, top of the pyramid: Call every customer whose predicted churn risk is above 13%, starting with month-to-month customers and the north; on this sample that saves about USD 21,700 compared with doing nothing. Then the supporting points: who is on the list (the coefficients), how sure we are (AUC 0.72, recall at 0.13), and what we assumed (the costs and that the offer works). 10 Your project this week ¶ Today we went from "how accurate is it?" to "what does each error cost?". That is exactly Advance 4 · The right metric , due Tuesday at 23:59. Case B (FinTrust Bank) does what we did today, with default instead of churned : a stratified split, a logistic regression, the confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 and AUC on the test set. Then choose a threshold with the cost of each error: approving a customer who defaults (you lose the loan) versus rejecting a good customer (you lose the interest you would have earned). Write down the two costs you assume and why. Case A (TalentCo) stays in regression, where the "right metric" question looks like this: 5-fold cross-validation of your linear regression, at least two coefficients interpreted in business terms (like our contract and support stories), and a justified choice between MAE and RMSE. RMSE punishes big misses more; is a big error on a salary worse than several small ones? Case C follows A or B depending on your target. Everyone: a table with the metrics so far (you will extend it in the final submission), and the key message of your presentation in one sentence , like our "call everyone above 13%". Next session: our logistic regression draws one smooth score, but churn hides thresholds such as "two or more tickets in the north". Can a decision tree, or a forest of them, do better? And how do we tell the story to the people who decide?

docs.text: The retention team has budget to call some customers with an offer, and it wants to know whom. By the end of this class you will have a model that gives every customer a probability of leaving, and a calling list chosen with money, not habit. ≈ 85 min 8 ideas Runs in your browser Advance 4
