docs.text: Last session the commercial team asked what drives a customer's monthly bill. A linear regression answered it: the plan, the data used and roaming explain about 92% of the variation in bills, and the model is off by about USD 3 on average. Today the retention team knocks on the door. Their question is different: will this customer cancel in the next three months? The answer is not a number of dollars but yes or no . That is a classification problem, and it needs a new model and, above all, new ways to judge it. We start from the clean customer base we built in session 2. In [1]: Copied! import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns CLEAN = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile_clean.csv" df = pd . read_csv ( CLEAN ) print ( f " { len ( df ) : , } customers, { df . shape [ 1 ] } columns" ) df . head () import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns CLEAN = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile_clean.csv" df = pd.read_csv(CLEAN) print(f"{len(df):,} customers, {df.shape[1]} columns") df.head() 4,985 customers, 15 columns Out[1]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id signup_date age region plan contract tenure_months data_gb call_minutes intl_roaming support_tickets autopay payment_method monthly_bill churned 0 CM-12254 2022-07-04 34 Metropolitana Basic 12 months 50 7.1 270 0 2 1 Unknown 25.46 0 1 CM-10173 2026-06-26 31 Centro Plus 12 months 3 19.0 310 0 0 0 Debit card 37.05 1 2 CM-11339 2020-05-29 38 Centro Prepaid Month-to-month 76 3.6 165 0 0 1 Credit card 11.43 0 3 CM-13440 2019-11-02 31 Centro Unlimited 12 months 82 17.8 248 0 2 0 Debit card 40.97 0 4 CM-10214 2022-07-01 34 Metropolitana Basic Month-to-month 50 4.3 240 0 0 0 Cash 19.18 1 In [2]: Copied! # The column we want to predict: 1 = cancelled within 3 months, 0 = stayed df [ "churned" ] . value_counts () # The column we want to predict: 1 = cancelled within 3 months, 0 = stayed df["churned"].value_counts() Out[2]: churned 0 4167 1 818 Name: count, dtype: int64
docs.title: 01 Previously at Cordillera Mobile

docs.text: Before any model, one number: how many customers actually leave? If churn is rare, a model can look brilliant while being useless. The usual score, accuracy , is the share of customers the model classifies correctly. It sounds like exactly what we want. Let's see. In [3]: Copied! churn_rate = df [ "churned" ] . mean () print ( f "Churn rate: { churn_rate : .1% } " ) print ( f "Customers who left: { df [ 'churned' ] . sum () : , } of { len ( df ) : , } " ) churn_rate = df["churned"].mean() print(f"Churn rate: {churn_rate:.1%}") print(f"Customers who left: {df['churned'].sum():,} of {len(df):,}") Churn rate: 16.4% Customers who left: 818 of 4,985 About one customer in six leaves. Now imagine the laziest possible "model": it says "stays" for everyone. It needs no data and no math. How accurate is it? Play with the explainer: slide the churn rate and run the lazy model on 100 customers. Watch what happens to accuracy and to the number of leavers it catches. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [4]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score , recall_score lazy = np . zeros ( len ( df ), dtype = int ) # predicts 0 ("stays") for everyone print ( f "Accuracy of 'nobody leaves': { accuracy_score ( df [ 'churned' ], lazy ) : .1% } " ) print ( f "Churners it catches (recall): { recall_score ( df [ 'churned' ], lazy ) : .0% } " ) from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score lazy = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=int) # predicts 0 ("stays") for everyone print(f"Accuracy of 'nobody leaves': {accuracy_score(df['churned'], lazy):.1%}") print(f"Churners it catches (recall): {recall_score(df['churned'], lazy):.0%}") Accuracy of 'nobody leaves': 83.6% Churners it catches (recall): 0% Business takeaway: a model that never calls anyone is right for 83.6% of customers and saves exactly zero of them. When one class is rare, accuracy mostly measures how rare it is. From now on we judge every churn model against this baseline, and with metrics that look at the churners themselves. {"q": "A colleague proudly reports a churn model with 83% accuracy on our customers. What is the first thing you ask?", "options": ["Nothing, 83% is a good grade", "How many of the customers who actually left does it catch?", "Whether it used more than ten features"], "answer": 1, "why": "Saying \"nobody leaves\" already scores 83.6% here. Accuracy alone cannot tell a useful model from that lazy one; recall on the churners can.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 The accuracy trap

docs.text: The recipe is the same as for the bill, with one change: the target is now churned . Out of X : customer_id (a label, not a behaviour), signup_date (already summarised by tenure_months ) and, of course, churned itself. Into X : everything we would know about a customer today , including monthly_bill . Last session it was the target; today it is a clue, because a surprisingly high bill might push someone out. In [5]: Copied! y = df [ "churned" ] X = df . drop ( columns = [ "customer_id" , "signup_date" , "churned" ]) print ( "Features:" , list ( X . columns )) y = df["churned"] X = df.drop(columns=["customer_id", "signup_date", "churned"]) print("Features:", list(X.columns)) Features: ['age', 'region', 'plan', 'contract', 'tenure_months', 'data_gb', 'call_minutes', 'intl_roaming', 'support_tickets', 'autopay', 'payment_method', 'monthly_bill'] Models only read numbers, so the text columns become dummies (0/1 columns), exactly as in session 3. We fix the order of plan and contract so that the dropped baseline is the simplest option: a Prepaid plan on a month-to-month contract. In [6]: Copied! X [ "plan" ] = pd . Categorical ( X [ "plan" ], [ "Prepaid" , "Basic" , "Plus" , "Unlimited" ]) X [ "contract" ] = pd . Categorical ( X [ "contract" ], [ "Month-to-month" , "12 months" , "24 months" ]) X = pd . get_dummies ( X , columns = [ "plan" , "contract" , "region" , "payment_method" ], drop_first = True , dtype = int ) print ( X . shape ) print ( list ( X . columns )) X["plan"] = pd.Categorical(X["plan"], ["Prepaid", "Basic", "Plus", "Unlimited"]) X["contract"] = pd.Categorical(X["contract"], ["Month-to-month", "12 months", "24 months"]) X = pd.get_dummies(X, columns=["plan", "contract", "region", "payment_method"], drop_first=True, dtype=int) print(X.shape) print(list(X.columns)) (4985, 20) ['age', 'tenure_months', 'data_gb', 'call_minutes', 'intl_roaming', 'support_tickets', 'autopay', 'monthly_bill', 'plan_Basic', 'plan_Plus', 'plan_Unlimited', 'contract_12 months', 'contract_24 months', 'region_Metropolitana', 'region_Norte', 'region_Sur', 'payment_method_Cash', 'payment_method_Credit card', 'payment_method_Debit card', 'payment_method_Unknown'] Now the train/test split, with one new argument: stratify=y . Only 16% of customers churn, so a random cut could, by bad luck, put more churners in one part than the other. Stratifying keeps the same churn rate in train and test , so the test set looks like the real customer base. In [7]: Copied! from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( X , y , test_size = 0.25 , stratify = y , random_state = 42 ) print ( f "Train: { len ( X_train ) : , } customers, churn rate { y_train . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "Test: { len ( X_test ) : , } customers, churn rate { y_test . mean () : .1% } " ) from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42 ) print(f"Train: {len(X_train):,} customers, churn rate {y_train.mean():.1%}") print(f"Test: {len(X_test):,} customers, churn rate {y_test.mean():.1%}") Train: 3,738 customers, churn rate 16.4% Test: 1,247 customers, churn rate 16.4% In [8]: Copied! # The same cut without stratify, for comparison _ , _ , y_tr_plain , y_te_plain = train_test_split ( X , y , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 42 ) print ( f "Without stratify: train { y_tr_plain . mean () : .1% } , test { y_te_plain . mean () : .1% } " ) # The same cut without stratify, for comparison _, _, y_tr_plain, y_te_plain = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42) print(f"Without stratify: train {y_tr_plain.mean():.1%}, test {y_te_plain.mean():.1%}") Without stratify: train 16.7%, test 15.6% Without stratify , the test set ends up with fewer churners than the training set. The gap looks small, but every metric we compute next depends on how many churners are in the test set. With a rare class, always stratify.
docs.title: 03 Preparing the data

docs.text: Why not reuse last week's linear regression, with churned (0 or 1) as the target? Its prediction would be a number we could read as "chance of leaving". Let's try it and look at the predictions. In [9]: Copied! from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression line = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) pred_line = line . predict ( X_test ) print ( f "Lowest prediction: { pred_line . min () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Highest prediction: { pred_line . max () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Customers with a 'probability' below 0: { ( pred_line < 0 ) . sum () } " ) from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression line = LinearRegression().fit(X_train, y_train) pred_line = line.predict(X_test) print(f"Lowest prediction: {pred_line.min():.2f}") print(f"Highest prediction: {pred_line.max():.2f}") print(f"Customers with a 'probability' below 0: {(pred_line < 0).sum()}") Lowest prediction: -0.18 Highest prediction: 0.62 Customers with a 'probability' below 0: 133 A probability of −0.18 means nothing. A straight line keeps going forever, so with enough tickets or enough tenure it leaves the range from 0 to 1. Logistic regression fixes this in two steps. First it computes a score exactly like a linear regression: $z = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots$ Then it squeezes that score through the sigmoid curve, $p = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$, which bends every number into the range 0 to 1. Large positive scores become probabilities near 1, large negative ones near 0, and a score of 0 becomes exactly 0.5. In the explainer, switch between the two models and move the weight and the intercept to reshape the S. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [10]: Copied! def sigmoid ( z ): return 1 / ( 1 + np . exp ( - z )) for z in [ - 4 , - 2 , 0 , 2 , 4 ]: print ( f "score z = { z : +d } → probability { sigmoid ( z ) : .2f } " ) def sigmoid(z): return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)) for z in [-4, -2, 0, 2, 4]: print(f"score z = {z:+d} → probability {sigmoid(z):.2f}") score z = -4 → probability 0.02 score z = -2 → probability 0.12 score z = +0 → probability 0.50 score z = +2 → probability 0.88 score z = +4 → probability 0.98 In [11]: Copied! z = np . linspace ( - 6 , 6 , 200 ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 3.5 )) plt . plot ( z , sigmoid ( z ), lw = 2.5 , label = "logistic: always between 0 and 1" ) plt . plot ( z , 0.5 + z / 8 , ls = "--" , label = "a straight line: leaves [0, 1]" ) plt . axhline ( 0 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . axhline ( 1 , color = "grey" , lw = 0.8 ) plt . ylim ( - 0.4 , 1.4 ) plt . title ( "The sigmoid squeezes any score into a probability" ) plt . xlabel ( "score z" ) plt . ylabel ( "predicted value" ) plt . legend () plt . show () z = np.linspace(-6, 6, 200) plt.figure(figsize=(7, 3.5)) plt.plot(z, sigmoid(z), lw=2.5, label="logistic: always between 0 and 1") plt.plot(z, 0.5 + z / 8, ls="--", label="a straight line: leaves [0, 1]") plt.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.axhline(1, color="grey", lw=0.8) plt.ylim(-0.4, 1.4) plt.title("The sigmoid squeezes any score into a probability") plt.xlabel("score z") plt.ylabel("predicted value") plt.legend() plt.show()
docs.title: 04 From a line to a probability

docs.text: In scikit-learn the model is LogisticRegression . We put a StandardScaler in front of it, inside a Pipeline . The scaler puts every feature on the same scale (mean 0, standard deviation 1), for two reasons: the solver that fits the model converges faster and more reliably when tenure (months) and call minutes (hundreds) are not on wildly different scales; later, the coefficients become comparable: each one says how much one standard deviation of that feature moves the score. The pipeline learns the scaling from the training set only, then applies it to any data you give it. In [12]: Copied! from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression model = Pipeline ([ ( "scale" , StandardScaler ()), ( "logit" , LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 2000 )), ]) model . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( "Trained on" , len ( X_train ), "customers" ) from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression model = Pipeline([ ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("logit", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)), ]) model.fit(X_train, y_train) print("Trained on", len(X_train), "customers") Trained on 3738 customers predict_proba returns two columns per customer: the probability of class 0 (stays) and of class 1 (leaves). We keep the second one. Here are six test customers with their probability of leaving. In [13]: Copied! p_test = model . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ] show = df . loc [ X_test . index , [ "customer_id" , "contract" , "tenure_months" , "support_tickets" , "region" , "churned" ]] . copy () show [ "p_churn" ] = p_test . round ( 2 ) show . sample ( 6 , random_state = 42 ) . sort_values ( "p_churn" , ascending = False ) p_test = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] show = df.loc[X_test.index, ["customer_id", "contract", "tenure_months", "support_tickets", "region", "churned"]].copy() show["p_churn"] = p_test.round(2) show.sample(6, random_state=42).sort_values("p_churn", ascending=False) Out[13]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id contract tenure_months support_tickets region churned p_churn 1372 CM-10824 Month-to-month 1 1 Sur 0 0.56 2473 CM-12797 Month-to-month 13 3 Metropolitana 1 0.47 4126 CM-11834 Month-to-month 43 1 Centro 1 0.12 4073 CM-14545 Month-to-month 76 0 Sur 0 0.08 956 CM-11709 24 months 14 0 Metropolitana 0 0.05 3353 CM-14086 12 months 56 0 Metropolitana 0 0.03 In [14]: Copied! plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) sns . histplot ( x = p_test , hue = y_test . map ({ 0 : "stayed" , 1 : "left" }), hue_order = [ "stayed" , "left" ], palette = { "stayed" : "tab:blue" , "left" : "tab:orange" }, bins = 30 , stat = "density" , common_norm = False , element = "step" ) plt . title ( "Predicted probability of leaving, test customers" ) plt . xlabel ( "predicted probability of churn" ) plt . ylabel ( "density" ) plt . show () plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4)) sns.histplot(x=p_test, hue=y_test.map({0: "stayed", 1: "left"}), hue_order=["stayed", "left"], palette={"stayed": "tab:blue", "left": "tab:orange"}, bins=30, stat="density", common_norm=False, element="step") plt.title("Predicted probability of leaving, test customers") plt.xlabel("predicted probability of churn") plt.ylabel("density") plt.show() The customers who really left (orange) tend to get higher probabilities, but the two groups overlap a lot. No single cut-off will separate them perfectly. That overlap is why the next two sections exist.
docs.title: 05 Training the logistic regression

docs.text: To turn probabilities into a decision we need a threshold : call the customer if $p \geq$ threshold. The default of model.predict() is 0.5. Each test customer then lands in one of four cells: True positive (TP): we call, and they were leaving. Money well spent. False positive (FP): we call, but they would have stayed. A wasted offer. False negative (FN): we don't call, and they leave. A lost customer. True negative (TN): we don't call, and they stay. Nothing happens. In [15]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix pred_05 = model . predict ( X_test ) # threshold 0.5 tn , fp , fn , tp = confusion_matrix ( y_test , pred_05 ) . ravel () print ( f "True positives (called, were leaving): { tp } " ) print ( f "False positives (called, would stay): { fp } " ) print ( f "False negatives (not called, left): { fn } " ) print ( f "True negatives (not called, stayed): { tn } " ) from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix pred_05 = model.predict(X_test) # threshold 0.5 tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_test, pred_05).ravel() print(f"True positives (called, were leaving): {tp}") print(f"False positives (called, would stay): {fp}") print(f"False negatives (not called, left): {fn}") print(f"True negatives (not called, stayed): {tn}") True positives (called, were leaving): 30 False positives (called, would stay): 10 False negatives (not called, left): 175 True negatives (not called, stayed): 1032 In [16]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 4.5 , 4 )) ConfusionMatrixDisplay . from_predictions ( y_test , pred_05 , display_labels = [ "stays" , "leaves" ], cmap = "Oranges" , colorbar = False , ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Threshold 0.5, test customers" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "predicted" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "actual" ) plt . show () from sklearn.metrics import ConfusionMatrixDisplay fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4)) ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions( y_test, pred_05, display_labels=["stays", "leaves"], cmap="Oranges", colorbar=False, ax=ax ) ax.set_title("Threshold 0.5, test customers") ax.set_xlabel("predicted") ax.set_ylabel("actual") plt.show() Each metric reads the matrix from a different angle: Precision = TP / (TP + FP): of the customers we call, how many were really leaving? How well do we spend the offers? Recall = TP / (TP + FN): of the customers who leave, how many do we call? How many leavers do we reach? F1 : a single number that balances the two (their harmonic mean). AUC : forget the threshold. Pick a random leaver and a random stayer: how often does the model give the leaver the higher probability? 0.5 is a coin flip, 1.0 is perfect. Session 5 draws the curve behind it. In [17]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import precision_score , f1_score , roc_auc_score print ( f "Accuracy: { accuracy_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .1% } (the lazy model: { 1 - y_test . mean () : .1% } )" ) print ( f "Precision: { precision_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } " ) print ( f "Recall: { recall_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } " ) print ( f "F1: { f1_score ( y_test , pred_05 ) : .2f } " ) print ( f "AUC: { roc_auc_score ( y_test , p_test ) : .2f } " ) from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, f1_score, roc_auc_score print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, pred_05):.1%} (the lazy model: {1 - y_test.mean():.1%})") print(f"Precision: {precision_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f}") print(f"Recall: {recall_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f}") print(f"F1: {f1_score(y_test, pred_05):.2f}") print(f"AUC: {roc_auc_score(y_test, p_test):.2f}") Accuracy: 85.2% (the lazy model: 83.6%) Precision: 0.75 Recall: 0.15 F1: 0.24 AUC: 0.72 In [18]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import classification_report print ( classification_report ( y_test , pred_05 , target_names = [ "stays" , "leaves" ])) from sklearn.metrics import classification_report print(classification_report(y_test, pred_05, target_names=["stays", "leaves"])) precision recall f1-score support stays 0.86 0.99 0.92 1042 leaves 0.75 0.15 0.24 205 accuracy 0.85 1247 macro avg 0.80 0.57 0.58 1247 weighted avg 0.84 0.85 0.81 1247 Read it like the retention manager would. When we call someone, we are right 3 times out of 4 (precision 0.75). But we only call 40 customers and reach 30 of the 205 leavers (recall 0.15). Accuracy (85.2%) barely beats the lazy model, yet the AUC of 0.72 says the ranking carries real signal. The problem is not the model; it is the threshold. The explainer below uses a toy example (customers buying a travel package), but the mechanism is identical: moving the threshold never changes the model, it moves customers between the cells of the matrix. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [19]: Copied! for t in [ 0.5 , 0.3 , 0.2 ]: pred_t = ( p_test >= t ) . astype ( int ) print ( f "threshold { t : .1f } : calls { pred_t . sum () : 4d } " f "precision { precision_score ( y_test , pred_t ) : .2f } recall { recall_score ( y_test , pred_t ) : .2f } " ) for t in [0.5, 0.3, 0.2]: pred_t = (p_test >= t).astype(int) print(f"threshold {t:.1f}: calls {pred_t.sum():4d} " f"precision {precision_score(y_test, pred_t):.2f} recall {recall_score(y_test, pred_t):.2f}") threshold 0.5: calls 40 precision 0.75 recall 0.15 threshold 0.3: calls 180 precision 0.39 recall 0.34 threshold 0.2: calls 341 precision 0.33 recall 0.55 {"q": "The retention team lowers the threshold from 0.5 to 0.2. What happens?", "options": ["Recall goes up and precision goes down: more leavers reached, more offers wasted", "Both precision and recall go up, because the model gets better", "Nothing changes: the threshold is part of the trained model"], "answer": 0, "why": "A lower bar means more customers get called. More of the leavers are among them (recall up), but so are more stayers (precision down). The model itself is untouched.", "code": false}
docs.title: 06 The confusion matrix

docs.text: 0.5 is a habit, not a decision. The right threshold depends on what each mistake costs Cordillera. Finance gives us two numbers: a missed churner (false negative) costs about USD 300 in lost margin; every offer costs about USD 40 , whether the customer was leaving or not. On a stayer it is simply wasted. We assume the offer keeps the leavers we call (optimistic, but a fine start). Then the total cost of a calling list is $$\text{cost} = 40 \times \text{customers called} + 300 \times \text{churners not called}.$$ In the explainer, the curve is that cost for every threshold, computed on our 1,247 test customers. Change the two costs and watch the cheapest threshold move. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [20]: Copied! COST_MISS = 300 # USD lost when a churner leaves without a call COST_OFFER = 40 # USD per call with an offer def total_cost ( threshold ): called = p_test >= threshold missed = ( ~ called ) & ( y_test . values == 1 ) return COST_OFFER * called . sum () + COST_MISS * missed . sum () print ( f "Call nobody: USD { COST_MISS * y_test . sum () : , } " ) print ( f "Call everyone: USD { COST_OFFER * len ( y_test ) : , } " ) print ( f "Threshold 0.5: USD { total_cost ( 0.5 ) : , } " ) COST_MISS = 300 # USD lost when a churner leaves without a call COST_OFFER = 40 # USD per call with an offer def total_cost(threshold): called = p_test >= threshold missed = (~called) & (y_test.values == 1) return COST_OFFER * called.sum() + COST_MISS * missed.sum() print(f"Call nobody: USD {COST_MISS * y_test.sum():,}") print(f"Call everyone: USD {COST_OFFER * len(y_test):,}") print(f"Threshold 0.5: USD {total_cost(0.5):,}") Call nobody: USD 61,500 Call everyone: USD 49,880 Threshold 0.5: USD 54,100 In [21]: Copied! thresholds = np . round ( np . arange ( 0.05 , 0.951 , 0.01 ), 2 ) costs = pd . Calling pays off as soon as $300p > 40$, that is $p > 40/300 \approx 0.13$. The break-even threshold is the ratio of the two costs. One honest caveat: we picked the threshold on the test set. docs.text: The retention team will ask why . Because we scaled the features, the coefficients are comparable: each one says how much a one-standard-deviation change in that feature pushes the score (and so the probability) of leaving. Positive pushes towards leaving, negative towards staying. The dummies compare against the baseline: a Prepaid customer on a month-to-month contract in the Centro region, paying by bank transfer. A 12- or 24-month contract has the strongest negative coefficients: those customers leave much less than month-to-month ones. Complaints and bills push out. More support_tickets and a higher monthly_bill raise the risk, and so does living in the Norte region. Loyalty and autopay protect. Longer tenure_months , autopay and an Unlimited plan go with staying. Age, call minutes and payment method barely matter. These are associations, not causes . The model says customers on contracts leave less; it does not prove that signing someone onto a contract will keep them. Still, it tells the team where to look. In [26]: Copied! # Checking two stories against the raw churn rates print ( df . groupby ( "contract" )[ "churned" ] . mean () . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) . to_string ()) print () norte = df [ "region" ] == "Norte" many_tickets = df [ "support_tickets" ] >= 2 print ( f "Norte, 2+ tickets: { df . loc [ norte & many_tickets , 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "Everyone else: { df . loc [ ~ ( norte & many_tickets ), 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( f "New customers (< 6 months): { df . loc [ df [ 'tenure_months' ] < 6 , 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) # Checking two stories against the raw churn rates print(df.groupby("contract")["churned"].mean().map("{:.1%}".format).to_string()) print() norte = df["region"] == "Norte" many_tickets = df["support_tickets"] >= 2 print(f"Norte, 2+ tickets: {df.loc[norte & many_tickets, 'churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"Everyone else: {df.loc[~(norte & many_tickets), 'churned'].mean():.1%}") print(f"New customers ( < 6 months): {df.loc[df['tenure_months'] < 6, 'churned'].mean():.1%}") contract 12 months 8.9% 24 months 7.8% Month-to-month 22.0% Norte, 2+ tickets: 51.1% Everyone else: 14.1% New customers (< 6 months): 44.4% The raw rates back it up, and they suggest three concrete actions: Offer contracts to month-to-month customers, the group with the highest churn. Fix support in the north : Norte customers with two or more complaints leave far more than anyone else. That is a coverage and service problem, not a pricing one. Look after new customers : in their first six months they leave at a much higher rate, so onboarding matters. Notice that some of these patterns are thresholds ("2 or more tickets", "under 6 months") that a single straight score handles only roughly. Keep that in mind for session 5. {"q": "The coefficient of autopay is negative. Calling everyone costs USD 49,880. The model at 0.5 is cheaper than nobody but worse than everyone, because it calls too few. The model at 0.13 calls 575 customers (46% of the base), reaches 149 of the 205 leavers and costs USD 39,800: USD 21,700 less than doing nothing and about USD 10,000 less than calling everyone. The message, top of the pyramid: Call every customer whose predicted churn risk is above 13%, starting with month-to-month customers and the north; on this sample that saves about USD 21,700 compared with doing nothing. Then the supporting points: who is on the list (the coefficients), how sure we are (AUC 0.72, recall at 0.13), and what we assumed (the costs and that the offer works).

docs.text: Today we went from "how accurate is it?" to "what does each error cost?". That is exactly Advance 4 · The right metric , due Tuesday at 23:59. Case B (FinTrust Bank) does what we did today, with default instead of churned : a stratified split, a logistic regression, the confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 and AUC on the test set. Then choose a threshold with the cost of each error: approving a customer who defaults (you lose the loan) versus rejecting a good customer (you lose the interest you would have earned). Write down the two costs you assume and why. Case A (TalentCo) stays in regression, where the "right metric" question looks like this: 5-fold cross-validation of your linear regression, at least two coefficients interpreted in business terms (like our contract and support stories), and a justified choice between MAE and RMSE. RMSE punishes big misses more; is a big error on a salary worse than several small ones? Case C follows A or B depending on your target. Everyone: a table with the metrics so far (you will extend it in the final submission), and the key message of your presentation in one sentence , like our "call everyone above 13%". Next session: our logistic regression draws one smooth score, but churn hides thresholds such as "two or more tickets in the north". Can a decision tree, or a forest of them, do better? And how do we tell the story to the people who decide?

A model that asks "Is the customer in the Norte? If yes, more than one ticket?" can. 02 How a tree chooses a question: Gini ¶ A decision tree splits customers with a question like tenure ≤ 5? To pick the question, it measures how mixed each group is with the Gini impurity : $$\text{Gini} = 1 - p_{\text{churn}}^2 - p_{\text{stay}}^2$$ A group where everybody stayed has Gini 0 (pure). A 50/50 group has Gini 0.5, the worst possible. After a split, the tree averages the two groups' Gini, weighted by their size , and keeps the question with the lowest weighted Gini. Drag the line yourself, then switch features. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Now the same arithmetic on Cordillera's training customers. Two kinds of randomness make the trees different from each other: Bootstrap samples: each tree trains on customers drawn at random with replacement , so some appear twice and about a third are left out. Random features: at each question, a tree may only look at a random handful of features, so not every tree starts with the obvious split. Each tree makes its own mistakes; averaged, the mistakes cancel out and the pattern stays. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Two simplifications in the explainer: it draws the features once per tree (scikit-learn draws them again at every question), and it counts hard votes (scikit-learn averages each tree's probability). The ROC curve shows, for every possible threshold, the share of churners you catch (true positive rate) against the share of loyal customers you bother (false positive rate). AUC is the area under it: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin toss. That sentence, not the AUC, is what the retention team will remember. The assumption of 3 in 10 is the team's, not the model's: say so on the slide, and show what happens if it is 1 in 10. 10 Telling the story: the pyramid principle ¶ You have 10 minutes with the retention director. A report tells the story in the order you did it: data, cleaning, charts, models, and the answer at minute nine. The pyramid principle turns it upside down: Key message first: one sentence with the answer and the action. Three supporting arguments: each one answers "why should I believe that?". Evidence under each argument: one chart or number per point, nothing that does not support an argument. If you are cut off at minute two, the director still has the answer. Build Cordillera's pyramid step by step, then flip it to report order to feel the difference. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. docs.title: Better models, a clearer story

docs.text: The retention team liked last week's churn model, but it reads every customer through one straight line. Today you try models that ask yes/no questions, compare them fairly, and turn the winner into a call list and a 10-minute story the team can act on. ≈ 85 min 11 ideas Runs in your browser Final submission
docs.title: Better models, a clearer story

docs.text: Last week you built a logistic regression for the retention team: it gives every customer a churn probability, and you learned to judge it with AUC instead of accuracy, because "nobody churns" is already about 83% accurate. Today's question: can a model that asks yes/no questions do better? Let's rebuild last week's starting point so this class stands on its own: the clean customer base, the same features, and the same 75/25 split stratified by churned , so the very same customers sit in the test set. In [1]: Copied! import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt CLEAN = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile_clean.csv" df = pd . read_csv ( CLEAN ) print ( f " { len ( df ) : , } customers, { df . shape [ 1 ] } columns" ) print ( f "Churn rate: { df [ 'churned' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt CLEAN = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hizocar/usm-course-intensivo/main/docs/datasets/cordillera_mobile_clean.csv" df = pd.read_csv(CLEAN) print(f"{len(df):,} customers, {df.shape[1]} columns") print(f"Churn rate: {df['churned'].mean():.1%}") 4,985 customers, 15 columns Churn rate: 16.4% In [2]: Copied! from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split # As in session 4: drop IDs and dates, one-hot encode the categories. # One change: we let pandas pick the reference categories, so month-to-month # gets its own column. A tree asks about one column at a time, so # "no contract?" becomes one question instead of two. X = pd . get_dummies ( df . drop ( columns = [ "customer_id" , "signup_date" , "churned" ]), columns = [ "region" , "plan" , "contract" , "payment_method" ], drop_first = True , dtype = int , ) y = df [ "churned" ] X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( X , y , test_size = 0.25 , stratify = y , random_state = 42 ) print ( f " { X . shape [ 1 ] } features · { len ( X_train ) : , } customers to train · { len ( X_test ) : , } to test" ) from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split # As in session 4: drop IDs and dates, one-hot encode the categories. # One change: we let pandas pick the reference categories, so month-to-month # gets its own column. A tree asks about one column at a time, so # "no contract?" becomes one question instead of two. X = pd.get_dummies( df.drop(columns=["customer_id", "signup_date", "churned"]), columns=["region", "plan", "contract", "payment_method"], drop_first=True, dtype=int, ) y = df["churned"] X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=42 ) print(f"{X.shape[1]} features · {len(X_train):,} customers to train · {len(X_test):,} to test") 20 features · 3,738 customers to train · 1,247 to test In [3]: Copied! from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score logit = make_pipeline ( StandardScaler (), LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 1000 )) logit . fit ( X_train , y_train ) auc_logit = roc_auc_score ( y_test , logit . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ]) print ( f "Logistic regression, test AUC: { auc_logit : .3f } <- the number to beat today" ) from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score logit = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)) logit.fit(X_train, y_train) auc_logit = roc_auc_score(y_test, logit.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]) print(f"Logistic regression, test AUC: {auc_logit:.3f} < - the number to beat today") Logistic regression, test AUC: 0.723 <- the number to beat today

docs.text: Logistic regression gives each feature one weight : every extra month as a customer, or every extra complaint, moves the risk by the same amount for everyone. Real behaviour often has thresholds (risk drops sharply after the first months) and interactions (complaints matter more in some regions). Let the data show you. In [4]: Copied! # Churn by tenure band: is the drop smooth, or is there a cliff? bands = pd . cut ( df [ "tenure_months" ], bins = [ 0 , 3 , 6 , 12 , 24 , 48 , 90 ], right = False ) by_band = df . groupby ( bands , observed = True )[ "churned" ] . mean () for band , rate in by_band . items (): print ( f "tenure { str ( band ) : >9 } months: { rate : 5.1% } churn" ) # Churn by tenure band: is the drop smooth, or is there a cliff? bands = pd.cut(df["tenure_months"], bins=[0, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 90], right=False) by_band = df.groupby(bands, observed=True)["churned"].mean() for band, rate in by_band.items(): print(f"tenure {str(band):>9} months: {rate:5.1%} churn") tenure [0, 3) months: 41.0% churn tenure [3, 6) months: 46.9% churn tenure [6, 12) months: 16.6% churn tenure [12, 24) months: 15.6% churn tenure [24, 48) months: 14.6% churn tenure [48, 90) months: 13.8% churn In [5]: Copied! # Complaints by region: does a second ticket mean the same everywhere? tickets = np . where ( df [ "support_tickets" ] >= 2 , "2+ tickets" , "0-1 tickets" ) table = df . pivot_table ( index = "region" , columns = tickets , values = "churned" , aggfunc = "mean" ) print (( table * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) . astype ( str ) + " %" ) # Complaints by region: does a second ticket mean the same everywhere? tickets = np.where(df["support_tickets"] >= 2, "2+ tickets", "0-1 tickets") table = df.pivot_table(index="region", columns=tickets, values="churned", aggfunc="mean") print((table * 100).round(1).astype(str) + " %") 0-1 tickets 2+ tickets region Centro 10.6 % 23.6 % Metropolitana 14.8 % 18.1 % Norte 12.5 % 51.1 % Sur 12.9 % 19.6 % Business takeaway: churn is not a smooth slope. New customers (under 6 months) leave far more often, and two or more complaints hurt much more in the Norte , where coverage is weaker. A single weight per feature cannot say "only in the north". A model that asks "Is the customer in the Norte? If yes, more than one ticket?" can.
docs.title: What a straight line misses

docs.text: A decision tree splits customers with a question like tenure ≤ 5? To pick the question, it measures how mixed each group is with the Gini impurity : $$\text{Gini} = 1 - p_{\text{churn}}^2 - p_{\text{stay}}^2$$ A group where everybody stayed has Gini 0 (pure). A 50/50 group has Gini 0.5, the worst possible. After a split, the tree averages the two groups' Gini, weighted by their size , and keeps the question with the lowest weighted Gini. Drag the line yourself, then switch features. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Now the same arithmetic on Cordillera's training customers. First, Gini itself: In [6]: Copied! def gini ( labels ): p = labels . mean () # share of customers that churned return 1 - p ** 2 - ( 1 - p ) ** 2 print ( f "Whole training set: Gini { gini ( y_train ) : .3f } " ) print ( f "A pure group (all stayed): Gini { gini ( pd . Series ([ 0 , 0 , 0 , 0 ])) : .3f } " ) print ( f "A 50/50 group: Gini { gini ( pd . Series ([ 0 , 1 , 0 , 1 ])) : .3f } " ) def gini(labels): p = labels.mean() # share of customers that churned return 1 - p**2 - (1 - p)**2 print(f"Whole training set: Gini {gini(y_train):.3f}") print(f"A pure group (all stayed): Gini {gini(pd.Series([0, 0, 0, 0])):.3f}") print(f"A 50/50 group: Gini {gini(pd.Series([0, 1, 0, 1])):.3f}") Whole training set: Gini 0.274 A pure group (all stayed): Gini 0.000 A 50/50 group: Gini 0.500 In [7]: Copied! def split_gini ( feature , threshold ): """Weighted Gini of the two groups made by 'feature <= threshold'.""" left = X_train [ feature ] <= threshold share_left = left . mean () return share_left * gini ( y_train [ left ]) + ( 1 - share_left ) * gini ( y_train [ ~ left ]) for feature , threshold in [( "tenure_months" , 5 ), ( "support_tickets" , 2 ), ( "age" , 40 )]: print ( f " { feature } <= { threshold : <3 } weighted Gini { split_gini ( feature , threshold ) : .4f } " ) def split_gini(feature, threshold): """Weighted Gini of the two groups made by 'feature < = threshold'.""" left = X_train[feature] < = threshold share_left = left.mean() return share_left * gini(y_train[left]) + (1 - share_left) * gini(y_train[~left]) for feature, threshold in [("tenure_months", 5), ("support_tickets", 2), ("age", 40)]: print(f"{feature} < = {threshold: < 3} weighted Gini {split_gini(feature, threshold):.4f}") tenure_months <= 5 weighted Gini 0.2622 support_tickets <= 2 weighted Gini 0.2617 age <= 40 weighted Gini 0.2742 Lower is better, but the differences look small because churn is only 16% of customers. The tree does not guess thresholds: it tries every one and keeps the best. That is all "training a tree" means. In [8]: Copied! for feature in [ "tenure_months" , "support_tickets" , "age" ]: candidates = sorted ( X_train [ feature ] . unique ())[: - 1 ] scores = { t : split_gini ( feature , t ) for t in candidates } best = min ( scores , key = scores . get ) print ( f "Best question on { feature : <16 } <= { best : <3 } weighted Gini { scores [ best ] : .4f } ( { len ( candidates ) } thresholds tried)" ) for feature in ["tenure_months", "support_tickets", "age"]: candidates = sorted(X_train[feature].unique())[:-1] scores = {t: split_gini(feature, t) for t in candidates} best = min(scores, key=scores.get) print(f"Best question on {feature: < 16} < = {best: < 3} weighted Gini {scores[best]:.4f} ({len(candidates)} thresholds tried)") Best question on tenure_months <= 5 weighted Gini 0.2622 (83 thresholds tried) Best question on support_tickets <= 2 weighted Gini 0.2617 (6 thresholds tried) Best question on age <= 25 weighted Gini 0.2737 (57 thresholds tried) {"q": "A group of customers in a tree has a Gini impurity of 0. What does that tell you?", "options": ["Nobody in the group churned", "Everyone in the group made the same choice: all churned or all stayed", "The split that made it was useless", "The group is exactly half churners, half stayers"], "answer": 1, "why": "Gini 0 means the group is pure: one class only. It could be all stayers or all churners. A 50/50 group is the opposite extreme, with Gini 0.5.", "code": false}
docs.title: 02 How a tree chooses a question: Gini

docs.text: A tree repeats the same move: find the best question, split, then do it again inside each group , until it reaches a maximum depth. The explainer below uses a toy example (will a customer buy a travel package, by age and income), but the mechanism is identical: each level adds one question per box, and each box predicts its majority class. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Now on our customers. max_depth=3 means at most three questions in a row, so at most 8 groups: small enough to read on a slide. In [9]: Copied! from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier , plot_tree tree3 = DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = 3 , random_state = 42 ) tree3 . fit ( X_train , y_train ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 17 , 7 )) plot_tree ( tree3 , feature_names = list ( X . columns ), class_names = [ "stays" , "churns" ], filled = True , rounded = True , fontsize = 9 ) plt . title ( "Churn tree, max_depth = 3 (left branch = condition true)" ) plt . show () from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree tree3 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42) tree3.fit(X_train, y_train) plt.figure(figsize=(17, 7)) plot_tree(tree3, feature_names=list(X.columns), class_names=["stays", "churns"], filled=True, rounded=True, fontsize=9) plt.title("Churn tree, max_depth = 3 (left branch = condition true)") plt.show()
docs.title: 03 Growing a tree

docs.text: Each box shows its question, its Gini, how many training customers reached it ( samples ), how many stayed and churned ( value ), and the majority class. Colour shows the majority: orange boxes say "stays", blue boxes say "churns", and paler means more mixed. The first question is support_tickets <= 2.5 : tickets beat tenure by a hair, exactly as your Gini loop found. Follow a path from the top and you get a rule a manager can read without any code. Let's check the churn rules on the training customers: In [10]: Copied! train = X_train . assign ( churned = y_train ) no_contract = train [ "contract_Month-to-month" ] == 1 norte = train [ "region_Norte" ] == 1 many_tickets = train [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 rules = { "3+ tickets, no contract, Norte" : many_tickets & no_contract & norte , "3+ tickets, no contract, other regions" : many_tickets & no_contract & ~ norte , "new (< 6 months), 0-2 tickets, no contract" : ( train [ "tenure_months" ] <= 5 ) & ~ many_tickets & no_contract , "everyone" : pd . Series ( True , index = train . index ), } for name , mask in rules . items (): print ( f " { name : <44 } { mask . sum () : >5, } customers churn { train . loc [ mask , 'churned' ] . mean () : 5.1% } " ) train = X_train.assign(churned=y_train) no_contract = train["contract_Month-to-month"] == 1 norte = train["region_Norte"] == 1 many_tickets = train["support_tickets"] >= 3 rules = { "3+ tickets, no contract, Norte": many_tickets & no_contract & norte, "3+ tickets, no contract, other regions": many_tickets & no_contract & ~norte, "new ( < 6 months), 0-2 tickets, no contract": (train["tenure_months"] < = 5) & ~many_tickets & no_contract, "everyone": pd.Series(True, index=train.index), } for name, mask in rules.items(): print(f"{name: < 44} {mask.sum():>5,} customers churn {train.loc[mask, 'churned'].mean():5.1%}") 3+ tickets, no contract, Norte 52 customers churn 88.5% 3+ tickets, no contract, other regions 52 customers churn 51.9% new (< 6 months), 0-2 tickets, no contract 137 customers churn 54.7% everyone 3,738 customers churn 16.4% In [11]: Copied! auc_tree3 = roc_auc_score ( y_test , tree3 . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ]) print ( f "Tree, depth 3: test AUC { auc_tree3 : .3f } " ) print ( f "Logistic regression: test AUC { auc_logit : .3f } " ) auc_tree3 = roc_auc_score(y_test, tree3.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]) print(f"Tree, depth 3: test AUC {auc_tree3:.3f}") print(f"Logistic regression: test AUC {auc_logit:.3f}") Tree, depth 3: test AUC 0.674 Logistic regression: test AUC 0.723 Business takeaway: the rules are excellent for a slide (unhappy, uncommitted customers in the north are the hottest group), but as a scorer this tree is worse than the line. With 8 leaves it can only give 8 different probabilities, so it ranks customers coarsely. Should we just let it grow deeper?
docs.title: Reading the tree as business rules

docs.text: Without max_depth , a tree keeps splitting until every leaf is pure, even if that leaf holds one customer. On the training data it is then always right . Look at what happens on customers it has never seen. In [12]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score full_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier ( random_state = 42 ) full_tree . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( f "Depth { full_tree . get_depth () } , { full_tree . get_n_leaves () : , } leaves for { len ( X_train ) : , } customers" ) print ( f "Accuracy train { accuracy_score ( y_train , full_tree . predict ( X_train )) : .3f } test { accuracy_score ( y_test , full_tree . predict ( X_test )) : .3f } " ) print ( f "AUC train { roc_auc_score ( y_train , full_tree . predict_proba ( X_train )[:, 1 ]) : .3f } test { roc_auc_score ( y_test , full_tree . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ]) : .3f } " ) from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score full_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42) full_tree.fit(X_train, y_train) print(f"Depth {full_tree.get_depth()}, {full_tree.get_n_leaves():,} leaves for {len(X_train):,} customers") print(f"Accuracy train {accuracy_score(y_train, full_tree.predict(X_train)):.3f} test {accuracy_score(y_test, full_tree.predict(X_test)):.3f}") print(f"AUC train {roc_auc_score(y_train, full_tree.predict_proba(X_train)[:, 1]):.3f} test {roc_auc_score(y_test, full_tree.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]):.3f}") Depth 26, 583 leaves for 3,738 customers Accuracy train 1.000 test 0.747 AUC train 1.000 test 0.563 A perfect score in training and a test accuracy below the "nobody churns" baseline of 83.6%: the tree has memorized the training customers, noise included. That is overfitting , the same problem you met with polynomials in session 3. The fix is to limit the depth. Which depth? Try them all. In [13]: Copied! rows = [] for depth in range ( 1 , 11 ): m = DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = depth , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( X_train , y_train ) rows . append ({ "max_depth" : depth , "train AUC" : roc_auc_score ( y_train , m . predict_proba ( X_train )[:, 1 ]), "test AUC" : roc_auc_score ( y_test , m . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ]), }) depths = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "max_depth" ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) plt . plot ( depths . index , depths [ "train AUC" ], marker = "o" , label = "train" ) plt . plot ( depths . index , depths [ "test AUC" ], marker = "o" , label = "test" ) plt . xlabel ( "max_depth" ) plt . ylabel ( "AUC" ) plt . title ( "Deeper trees fit training data better, not new customers" ) plt . legend () plt . show () print ( depths . round ( 3 ) . We pick the peak. (Strictly, you should choose the depth with cross-validation on the training set, as in session 4, and touch the test set only once at the end. With a small search like this one, the conclusion is the same.) Even the best single tree stays below the logistic regression. One tree is unstable : change a few customers and the first question can change, and everything under it with it. docs.title: 04 When trees memorize

docs.text: A random forest grows hundreds of trees and lets them vote. Two kinds of randomness make the trees different from each other: Bootstrap samples: each tree trains on customers drawn at random with replacement , so some appear twice and about a third are left out. Random features: at each question, a tree may only look at a random handful of features, so not every tree starts with the obvious split. Each tree makes its own mistakes; averaged, the mistakes cancel out and the pattern stays. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. Two simplifications in the explainer: it draws the features once per tree (scikit-learn draws them again at every question), and it counts hard votes (scikit-learn averages each tree's probability). The idea is the same. Now on the real data, with 200 trees. min_samples_leaf=5 stops any leaf from holding fewer than 5 customers, a gentler brake than max_depth . In [15]: Copied! from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier forest = RandomForestClassifier ( n_estimators = 200 , min_samples_leaf = 5 , random_state = 42 ) forest . fit ( X_train , y_train ) auc_forest = roc_auc_score ( y_test , forest . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ]) print ( f "Random forest (200 trees): test AUC { auc_forest : .3f } " ) print ( f "Best single tree: test AUC { depths [ 'test AUC' ] . max () : .3f } " ) print ( f "Logistic regression: test AUC { auc_logit : .3f } " ) from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=42) forest.fit(X_train, y_train) auc_forest = roc_auc_score(y_test, forest.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]) print(f"Random forest (200 trees): test AUC {auc_forest:.3f}") print(f"Best single tree: test AUC {depths['test AUC'].max():.3f}") print(f"Logistic regression: test AUC {auc_logit:.3f}") Random forest (200 trees): test AUC 0.737 Best single tree: test AUC 0.690 Logistic regression: test AUC 0.723 Let's look inside the forest for one test customer, a close call. Each tree gives its own churn probability; the forest's answer is their average. In [16]: Copied! p_forest = pd . Series ( forest . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ], index = X_test . index ) who = ( p_forest - 0.5 ) . abs () . idxmin () # the customer closest to 50/50 customer = X_test . loc [[ who ]] . to_numpy () per_tree = np . array ([ t . predict_proba ( customer )[ 0 , 1 ] for t in forest . estimators_ ]) print ( f "Customer { df . loc [ who , 'customer_id' ] } : { df . loc [ who , 'tenure_months' ] } months, " f " { df . loc [ who , 'support_tickets' ] } tickets, { df . loc [ who , 'contract' ] } , { df . loc [ who , 'region' ] } " ) print ( "First 10 trees:" , np . round ( per_tree [: 10 ], 2 )) print ( f "Trees range from { per_tree . min () : .2f } to { per_tree . max () : .2f } ; " f " { ( per_tree >= 0.5 ) . sum () } of { len ( per_tree ) } lean 'churn'" ) print ( f "Average of the 200 trees = forest probability: { per_tree . mean () : .3f } (predict_proba says { p_forest [ who ] : .3f } )" ) p_forest = pd.Series(forest.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1], index=X_test.index) who = (p_forest - 0.5).abs().idxmin() # the customer closest to 50/50 customer = X_test.loc[[who]].to_numpy() per_tree = np.array([t.predict_proba(customer)[0, 1] for t in forest.estimators_]) print(f"Customer {df.loc[who, 'customer_id']}: {df.loc[who, 'tenure_months']} months, " f"{df.loc[who, 'support_tickets']} tickets, {df.loc[who, 'contract']}, {df.loc[who, 'region']}") print("First 10 trees:", np.round(per_tree[:10], 2)) print(f"Trees range from {per_tree.min():.2f} to {per_tree.max():.2f}; " f"{(per_tree >= 0.5).sum()} of {len(per_tree)} lean 'churn'") print(f"Average of the 200 trees = forest probability: {per_tree.mean():.3f} (predict_proba says {p_forest[who]:.3f})") Customer CM-10060: 5 months, 0 tickets, Month-to-month, Metropolitana First 10 trees: [0.82 0.7 0.69 0.41 0. 0.8 1. 0.88 0.08 0.11] Trees range from 0.00 to 1.00; 100 of 200 lean 'churn' Average of the 200 trees = forest probability: 0.499 (predict_proba says 0.499)
docs.title: 05 A forest: many trees voting

docs.text: The retention team will ask "so what drives churn?" . A forest answers with feature importance : how much each feature lowered the Gini, summed over every question in every tree. In [17]: Copied! importance = pd . Series ( forest . feature_importances_ , index = X . columns ) . sort_values () plt . figure ( figsize = ( 7 , 5 )) importance . tail ( 10 ) . plot . barh ( color = "#c85a24" ) plt . xlabel ( "share of the total Gini decrease" ) plt . title ( "Random forest: top 10 features for churn" ) plt . show () importance = pd.Series(forest.feature_importances_, index=X.columns).sort_values() plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5)) importance.tail(10).plot.barh(color="#c85a24") plt.xlabel("share of the total Gini decrease") plt.title("Random forest: top 10 features for churn") plt.show() One caution before you put that chart on a slide: Gini importance favours numeric features with many possible thresholds (bill, data, minutes), even when they help little. A sturdier check is permutation importance on the test set: shuffle one column, and see how much the test AUC drops. If nothing drops, the model did not really need that feature. In [18]: Copied! from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance perm = permutation_importance ( forest , X_test , y_test , scoring = "roc_auc" , n_repeats = 5 , random_state = 42 ) perm_imp = pd . Series ( perm . importances_mean , index = X . columns ) . sort_values ( ascending = False ) print ( "Drop in test AUC when the column is shuffled:" ) for feature , drop in perm_imp . head ( 8 ) . items (): print ( f " { feature : <26 } { drop : +.3f } " ) from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance perm = permutation_importance(forest, X_test, y_test, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=5, random_state=42) perm_imp = pd.Series(perm.importances_mean, index=X.columns).sort_values(ascending=False) print("Drop in test AUC when the column is shuffled:") for feature, drop in perm_imp.head(8).items(): print(f" {feature: < 26} {drop:+.3f}") Drop in test AUC when the column is shuffled: support_tickets +0.051 contract_Month-to-month +0.048 tenure_months +0.032 autopay +0.018 region_Norte +0.013 plan_Unlimited +0.005 monthly_bill +0.004 plan_Plus +0.004 Importance says how much a feature matters, never in which direction . Check the direction with a simple table before you write a recommendation: In [19]: Copied! checks = { "new customer (< 6 months)" : df [ "tenure_months" ] < 6 , "3+ support tickets" : df [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 , "no contract (month-to-month)" : df [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" , "Norte with 2+ tickets" : ( df [ "region" ] == "Norte" ) & ( df [ "support_tickets" ] >= 2 ), "autopay" : df [ "autopay" ] == 1 , } for name , mask in checks . items (): print ( f " { name : <30 } churn { df . loc [ mask , 'churned' ] . mean () : 5.1% } vs { df . loc [ ~ mask , 'churned' ] . mean () : 5.1% } for the rest" ) checks = { "new customer ( < 6 months)": df["tenure_months"] < 6, "3+ support tickets": df["support_tickets"] >= 3, "no contract (month-to-month)": df["contract"] == "Month-to-month", "Norte with 2+ tickets": (df["region"] == "Norte") & (df["support_tickets"] >= 2), "autopay": df["autopay"] == 1, } for name, mask in checks.items(): print(f"{name: < 30} churn {df.loc[mask, 'churned'].mean():5.1%} vs {df.loc[~mask, 'churned'].mean():5.1%} for the rest") new customer (< 6 months) churn 44.4% vs 14.5% for the rest 3+ support tickets churn 49.8% vs 14.5% for the rest no contract (month-to-month) churn 22.0% vs 8.5% for the rest Norte with 2+ tickets churn 51.1% vs 14.1% for the rest autopay churn 12.1% vs 19.9% for the rest Business takeaway, translated into actions: Permutation importance puts support tickets , no contract and tenure on top, and tickets and tenure also lead the Gini chart. Bill, data and minutes look important in the Gini chart, yet shuffling them barely moves the test AUC: that is the bias from the caution above, in action. Support tickets (above all in the Norte): the third ticket is an alarm. Action: escalate customers with 3+ tickets, and fix coverage complaints in the north first. No contract: customers who can leave any day, do. Action: offer month-to-month customers at risk a 12-month contract with a discount. Tenure: the first six months decide. Action: an onboarding call in months 1 to 3. Caution: importance is not causation. Autopay customers churn less, but switching someone to autopay will not necessarily keep them; they may simply be more committed customers to begin with.
docs.title: 06 Which features matter

docs.text: A fair comparison uses the same test customers and a metric that does not depend on one threshold. The ROC curve shows, for every possible threshold, the share of churners you catch (true positive rate) against the share of loyal customers you bother (false positive rate). AUC is the area under it: 1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is a coin toss. The explainer uses toy buyers and non-buyers; the mechanism is the same for churners. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. In [20]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve tree_best = DecisionTreeClassifier ( max_depth = best_depth , random_state = 42 ) . fit ( X_train , y_train ) models = { "Logistic regression" : logit , f "Decision tree (depth { best_depth } )" : tree_best , "Random forest" : forest , } plt . figure ( figsize = ( 6 , 6 )) for name , model in models . items (): p = model . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ] fpr , tpr , _ = roc_curve ( y_test , p ) plt . plot ( fpr , tpr , label = f " { name } (AUC { roc_auc_score ( y_test , p ) : .3f } )" ) plt . plot ([ 0 , 1 ], [ 0 , 1 ], "--" , color = "grey" , label = "coin toss (AUC 0.5)" ) plt . xlabel ( "False positive rate (loyal customers called)" ) plt . ylabel ( "True positive rate (churners caught)" ) plt . title ( f "Churn models on the same { len ( y_test ) : , } test customers" ) plt . legend ( loc = "lower right" ) plt . show () from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve tree_best = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=best_depth, random_state=42).fit(X_train, y_train) models = { "Logistic regression": logit, f"Decision tree (depth {best_depth})": tree_best, "Random forest": forest, } plt.figure(figsize=(6, 6)) for name, model in models.items(): p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, p) plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{name} (AUC {roc_auc_score(y_test, p):.3f})") plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", color="grey", label="coin toss (AUC 0.5)") plt.xlabel("False positive rate (loyal customers called)") plt.ylabel("True positive rate (churners caught)") plt.title(f"Churn models on the same {len(y_test):,} test customers") plt.legend(loc="lower right") plt.show() The comparison table is what goes into your notebook and onto a slide. Next to AUC, add one number the business understands: if the team calls the 10% of customers the model ranks riskiest , what share of all churners does it reach? In [21]: Copied! from sklearn.metrics import precision_score , recall_score def caught_in_top ( p , share = 0.10 ): top = p >= np . quantile ( p , 1 - share ) return y_test [ top ] . sum () / y_test . sum () rows = [] for name , model in models . items (): p = model . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ] pred = ( p >= 0.5 ) . astype ( int ) rows . append ({ "model" : name , "test AUC" : roc_auc_score ( y_test , p ), "accuracy" : accuracy_score ( y_test , pred ), "precision" : precision_score ( y_test , pred , zero_division = 0 ), "recall" : recall_score ( y_test , pred ), "churners in top 10%" : caught_in_top ( p ), }) comparison = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "model" ) . round ( 3 ) comparison from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score def caught_in_top(p, share=0.10): top = p >= np.quantile(p, 1 - share) return y_test[top].sum() / y_test.sum() rows = [] for name, model in models.items(): p = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] pred = (p >= 0.5).astype(int) rows.append({ "model": name, "test AUC": roc_auc_score(y_test, p), "accuracy": accuracy_score(y_test, pred), "precision": precision_score(y_test, pred, zero_division=0), "recall": recall_score(y_test, pred), "churners in top 10%": caught_in_top(p), }) comparison = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model").round(3) comparison Out[21]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } test AUC accuracy precision recall churners in top 10% model Logistic regression 0.723 0.852 0.750 0.146 0.278 Decision tree (depth 7) 0.690 0.839 0.527 0.190 0.268 Random forest 0.737 0.845 0.667 0.117 0.322 The forest has the best AUC and reaches the most churners with the same number of calls. Notice how little accuracy, precision and recall at the default 0.5 threshold tell you here: with 16% churners, every model predicts "churn" rarely at 0.5. That is why you choose a threshold with the business (session 4) and compare models with AUC.
docs.title: 07 Comparing models fairly: ROC and AUC

docs.text: Could other settings do better? GridSearchCV tries each combination with cross-validation on the training set only . Keep searches small: here 6 combinations × 3 folds = 18 forests of 100 trees. In [22]: Copied! from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV search = GridSearchCV ( RandomForestClassifier ( n_estimators = 100 , random_state = 42 ), param_grid = { "max_depth" : [ 6 , 10 , None ], "min_samples_leaf" : [ 5 , 20 ]}, scoring = "roc_auc" , cv = 3 , ) search . fit ( X_train , y_train ) print ( "Best settings:" , search . best_params_ ) print ( f "Cross-validated AUC (train): { search . best_score_ : .3f } " ) print ( f "Test AUC of the tuned forest: { roc_auc_score ( y_test , search . predict_proba ( X_test )[:, 1 ]) : .3f } (ours: { auc_forest : .3f } )" ) from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV search = GridSearchCV( RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42), param_grid={"max_depth": [6, 10, None], "min_samples_leaf": [5, 20]}, scoring="roc_auc", cv=3, ) search.fit(X_train, y_train) print("Best settings:", search.best_params_) print(f"Cross-validated AUC (train): {search.best_score_:.3f}") print(f"Test AUC of the tuned forest: {roc_auc_score(y_test, search.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]):.3f} (ours: {auc_forest:.3f})") Best settings: {'max_depth': 6, 'min_samples_leaf': 20} Cross-validated AUC (train): 0.768 Test AUC of the tuned forest: 0.739 (ours: 0.737) Tuning moves the AUC in the third decimal. That is typical: the choice of model family and good features matter far more than fine settings . We keep our 200-tree forest. {"q": "A new churn model has a test AUC of 0.50. What does that mean?", "options": ["It catches half of the churners", "It ranks customers no better than a coin toss", "It is 50% accurate", "It needs a threshold of 0.5"], "answer": 1, "why": "AUC is the probability that a random churner gets a higher score than a random loyal customer. At 0.5 the scores carry no information: the ROC curve sits on the diagonal.", "code": false}
docs.title: A light tune-up (optional)

docs.text: Trees also predict numbers. A RandomForestRegressor averages the bills of the customers in each leaf instead of voting. Let's compare it with session 3's linear regression on monthly_bill , on session 3's own split. In [23]: Copied! from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , r2_score X_bill = X . drop ( columns = [ "monthly_bill" ]) y_bill = df [ "monthly_bill" ] # Session 3's split: 70/30, random_state=42 Xb_train , Xb_test , yb_train , yb_test = train_test_split ( X_bill , y_bill , test_size = 0.3 , random_state = 42 ) bill_models = { "Linear regression" : LinearRegression (), "Random forest" : RandomForestRegressor ( n_estimators = 200 , min_samples_leaf = 5 , random_state = 42 ), } rows = [] for name , model in bill_models . items (): model . fit ( Xb_train , yb_train ) pred = model . predict ( Xb_test ) rows . append ({ "model" : name , "test MAE (USD)" : mean_absolute_error ( yb_test , pred ), "test R²" : r2_score ( yb_test , pred )}) pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "model" ) . round ( 3 ) from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score X_bill = X.drop(columns=["monthly_bill"]) y_bill = df["monthly_bill"] # Session 3's split: 70/30, random_state=42 Xb_train, Xb_test, yb_train, yb_test = train_test_split(X_bill, y_bill, test_size=0.3, random_state=42) bill_models = { "Linear regression": LinearRegression(), "Random forest": RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=200, min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=42), } rows = [] for name, model in bill_models.items(): model.fit(Xb_train, yb_train) pred = model.predict(Xb_test) rows.append({"model": name, "test MAE (USD)": mean_absolute_error(yb_test, pred), "test R²": r2_score(yb_test, pred)}) pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model").round(3) Out[23]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } test MAE (USD) test R² model Linear regression 2.870 0.924 Random forest 2.696 0.931 Here the line was already very good, because a bill really is a sum (plan price plus a price per GB plus roaming…). The forest still shaves a little off the error by catching that Unlimited plans charge almost nothing per extra GB, a kink the straight line averages away. But the linear model keeps one big advantage for the commercial team: its coefficients read as prices. Case A teams (TalentCo): this is your second model. Same split, RandomForestRegressor next to your linear regression, MAE, RMSE and R² in one table, and a sentence on whether the gain is worth losing the coefficients.
docs.title: 08 For the commercial team: trees for the bill

docs.text: A model is only useful when it changes what someone does on Monday. The retention team can call about 10% of customers a month . Score the test customers, whom the model has never seen, and build the list. In [24]: Copied! scored = df . loc [ X_test . index , [ "customer_id" , "tenure_months" , "support_tickets" , "contract" , "region" , "monthly_bill" , "churned" ]] . copy () scored [ "risk" ] = p_forest call_list = scored . sort_values ( "risk" , ascending = False ) . head ( int ( len ( scored ) * 0.10 )) print ( f "Call list: { len ( call_list ) } of { len ( scored ) } test customers" ) call_list . drop ( columns = "churned" ) . head ( 10 ) . round ({ "risk" : 2 }) scored = df.loc[X_test.index, ["customer_id", "tenure_months", "support_tickets", "contract", "region", "monthly_bill", "churned"]].copy() scored["risk"] = p_forest call_list = scored.sort_values("risk", ascending=False).head(int(len(scored) * 0.10)) print(f"Call list: {len(call_list)} of {len(scored)} test customers") call_list.drop(columns="churned").head(10).round({"risk": 2}) Call list: 124 of 1247 test customers Out[24]: .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } customer_id tenure_months support_tickets contract region monthly_bill risk 2549 CM-12403 26 4 Month-to-month Norte 12.92 0.73 2426 CM-13952 6 3 Month-to-month Norte 12.45 0.72 2033 CM-10058 10 3 Month-to-month Norte 28.07 0.72 4596 CM-13537 32 3 Month-to-month Norte 11.83 0.71 2003 CM-12652 29 3 Month-to-month Norte 19.31 0.70 1170 CM-10001 58 3 Month-to-month Norte 13.27 0.68 4452 CM-12581 67 3 Month-to-month Norte 39.77 0.67 64 CM-11129 3 3 Month-to-month Metropolitana 33.32 0.67 589 CM-10980 7 4 Month-to-month Norte 32.60 0.66 846 CM-14077 9 3 Month-to-month Norte 23.17 0.66 In [25]: Copied! caught = call_list [ "churned" ] . sum () random_hit = scored [ "churned" ] . mean () * len ( call_list ) print ( f "Real churners on the list: { caught } of { len ( call_list ) } ( { caught / len ( call_list ) : .0% } of calls)" ) print ( f "Calling { len ( call_list ) } customers at random would reach about { random_hit : .0f } " ) print ( f "That is { caught / random_hit : .1f } × more churners per call" ) caught = call_list["churned"].sum() random_hit = scored["churned"].mean() * len(call_list) print(f"Real churners on the list: {caught} of {len(call_list)} ({caught / len(call_list):.0%} of calls)") print(f"Calling {len(call_list)} customers at random would reach about {random_hit:.0f}") print(f"That is {caught / random_hit:.1f}× more churners per call") Real churners on the list: 66 of 124 (53% of calls) Calling 124 customers at random would reach about 20 That is 3.2× more churners per call Who is on the list? Compare its profile with the whole test set; this becomes the description of the target group on your slide. In [26]: Copied! def profile ( group ): return pd . Series ({ "no contract" : ( group [ "contract" ] == "Month-to-month" ) . mean (), "new (< 6 months)" : ( group [ "tenure_months" ] < 6 ) . mean (), "3+ tickets" : ( group [ "support_tickets" ] >= 3 ) . mean (), "Norte" : ( group [ "region" ] == "Norte" ) . mean (), }) traits = pd . Assume, as the retention team does, that a call with an offer keeps 3 in 10 of the churners it reaches. Scale the test set (a quarter of the base) up to all customers. In [27]: Copied! SAVE_RATE = 0.30 # retention team's assumption: 3 in 10 called churners stay scale_up = len ( df ) / len ( scored ) # the test set is a quarter of the customer base calls = len ( call_list ) * scale_up saved_model = caught * SAVE_RATE * scale_up saved_random = random_hit * SAVE_RATE * scale_up print ( f "Calls per month across the base: about { calls : .0f } " ) print ( f "Customers kept with the model's list: about { saved_model : .0f } " ) print ( f "Customers kept with a random list: about { saved_random : .0f } " ) SAVE_RATE = 0.30 # retention team's assumption: 3 in 10 called churners stay scale_up = len(df) / len(scored) # the test set is a quarter of the customer base calls = len(call_list) * scale_up saved_model = caught * SAVE_RATE * scale_up saved_random = random_hit * SAVE_RATE * scale_up print(f"Calls per month across the base: about {calls:.0f}") print(f"Customers kept with the model's list: about {saved_model:.0f}") print(f"Customers kept with a random list: about {saved_random:.0f}") Calls per month across the base: about 496 Customers kept with the model's list: about 79 Customers kept with a random list: about 24 Business takeaway: same number of calls, more than three times the customers kept. docs.title: 09 From model to decision

docs.text: You have 10 minutes with the retention director. A report tells the story in the order you did it: data, cleaning, charts, models, and the answer at minute nine. The pyramid principle turns it upside down: Key message first: one sentence with the answer and the action. Three supporting arguments: each one answers "why should I believe that?". Evidence under each argument: one chart or number per point, nothing that does not support an argument. If you are cut off at minute two, the director still has the answer. Build Cordillera's pyramid step by step, then flip it to report order to feel the difference. ▶ Interactive explainer: open this class on the course website to use it. For a longer walkthrough with more examples, open the interactive class on pyramid presentations . Here is Cordillera's pyramid written with the numbers this notebook computed, so the story and the evidence never drift apart: In [28]: Copied! pyramid = { "key message" : f "Call the { len ( call_list ) / len ( scored ) : .0% } of customers our forest flags each month: " f "it reaches { caught / random_hit : .1f } x more future churners than calling at random." , "arguments" : { "1. Churn is predictable" : [ f "ROC chart: forest AUC { auc_forest : .2f } vs logistic { auc_logit : .2f } vs coin 0.50" , "Comparison table of the three models" , ], "2. Three groups carry most of the risk" : [ "Feature importance: tickets, no contract, tenure" , "Churn table: new customers, 3+ tickets, Norte with 2+ tickets" , ], "3. A targeted list pays off" : [ f "Call list: { caught } churners in { len ( call_list ) } calls vs { random_hit : .0f } at random" , f "About { saved_model : .0f } customers kept per month vs { saved_random : .0f } (if 3 in 10 are saved)" , ], }, } print ( "KEY MESSAGE:" , pyramid [ "key message" ]) for argument , evidence in pyramid [ "arguments" ] . items (): print ( " \n " + argument ) for item in evidence : print ( " -" , item ) pyramid = { "key message": f"Call the {len(call_list) / len(scored):.0%} of customers our forest flags each month: " f"it reaches {caught / random_hit:.1f}x more future churners than calling at random.", "arguments": { "1. Churn is predictable": [ f"ROC chart: forest AUC {auc_forest:.2f} vs logistic {auc_logit:.2f} vs coin 0.50", "Comparison table of the three models", ], "2. Three groups carry most of the risk": [ "Feature importance: tickets, no contract, tenure", "Churn table: new customers, 3+ tickets, Norte with 2+ tickets", ], "3. A targeted list pays off": [ f"Call list: {caught} churners in {len(call_list)} calls vs {random_hit:.0f} at random", f"About {saved_model:.0f} customers kept per month vs {saved_random:.0f} (if 3 in 10 are saved)", ], }, } print("KEY MESSAGE:", pyramid["key message"]) for argument, evidence in pyramid["arguments"].items(): print("\n" + argument) for item in evidence: print(" -", item) KEY MESSAGE: Call the 10% of customers our forest flags each month: it reaches 3.2x more future churners than calling at random. 1. Churn is predictable - ROC chart: forest AUC 0.74 vs logistic 0.72 vs coin 0.50 - Comparison table of the three models 2. Three groups carry most of the risk - Feature importance: tickets, no contract, tenure - Churn table: new customers, 3+ tickets, Norte with 2+ tickets 3. A targeted list pays off - Call list: 66 churners in 124 calls vs 20 at random - About 79 customers kept per month vs 24 (if 3 in 10 are saved) A 10-minute plan for that pyramid: Minute What you say What is on screen 0–1 The key message and the action you ask for One sentence, nothing else 1–3 Argument 1: churn is predictable ROC curves and the comparison table 3–6 Argument 2: three groups carry the risk Importance chart and the churn table 6–8 Argument 3: the list pays off Call list profile and customers kept 8–9 Limitations: simulated save rate, one snapshot, importance ≠ causation Short list 9–10 The key message again, and the next step The same sentence as minute 0 Data cleaning and the code do not get a slide of their own: they live in the notebook, and you mention them only if someone asks. {"q": "In a pyramid-structured presentation, what goes at the top, in the first minute?", "options": ["The data source and how it was cleaned", "The model comparison table", "The key message: the answer and the action you recommend", "The limitations of the analysis"], "answer": 2, "why": "The pyramid starts with the conclusion. Arguments and evidence come after it, to support it. Data and cleaning go in the notebook, not at the top of the story.", "code": false}

FacetGrid ( iris , col = 'species' , height = 4 ) g . map ( sns . scatterplot , 'sepal_length' , 'sepal_width' , alpha = 0.7 ) g . set_axis_labels ( 'Sepal length' , 'Sepal width' ) g . set_titles ( col_template = ' {col_name} ' ) plt . show () # One scatter plot per species, side by side g = sns.FacetGrid(iris, col='species', height=4) g.map(sns.scatterplot, 'sepal_length', 'sepal_width', alpha=0.7) g.set_axis_labels('Sepal length', 'Sepal width') g.set_titles(col_template='{col_name}') plt.show()
